docs.title: pgfs: a PostgreSQL-backed FUSE filesystem
docs.text:
pgfs mounts a directory tree whose files and directories are rows in a PostgreSQL database. Ordinary programs (cp, git, editors, build tools) read and write it like any local directory; SQL clients see the same data as tables.

nix develop
./scripts/pgfs.sh up                          # PostgreSQL + build + mount at testdata/mnt
echo hello > testdata/mnt/hello.txt
psql -h "$PWD/testdata" -d pgfs -c "SELECT parent, name, size FROM entries"
./scripts/pgfs.sh down

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
1. Your first pgfs mount gets a mount running in five minutes.
  2. Regular Files, Directory Trees and Atomic Rename cover everyday use.
  3. Reliable Mount and Observability are for running pgfs and diagnosing it.
  4. Regular Files: Explanation explains the storage model everything else builds on.

docs.title: Feature summaries
docs.text:
• Project-Local Development Environment: A contributor goes from a fresh clone to a live pgfs mount with one command. The Postgres cluster, the mount point, the logs and the pid files all live under the project's testdata/ directory, so nothing touches a system-wide Postgres and rm -rf testdata is a full reset.
  • Regular Files: Users can create, read, write, and delete files through standard POSIX file operations on the mounted directory.
  • Directory Trees: Users can create nested directories, list their contents, and remove empty directories through standard POSIX directory operations.
  • Atomic Rename: Users can rename (move) files and directories with standard mv semantics, including overwriting existing files and empty directories.
  • Reliable Mount & Shutdown: The filesystem mounts and unmounts cleanly. Crashing or killing the daemon never leaves a ghost mount behind.
  • Observability & Diagnostics: Operators can see what the daemon is doing, how fast it is doing it, and why something failed, from the log alone: structured spans for every operation, periodic metrics, an on-demand state dump, and self-contained error chains and crash reports.
  • On-Demand Profiling: Operators can profile a running pgfs daemon without restarting it: SIGUSR2 starts and stops a CPU sampler that writes a flamegraph, and a span trace of every FUSE callback and database call is written on shutdown. All of it is compiled in only with the profiling feature.
  • Replicated Storage: A pgfs mount can be backed by a primary Postgres and a physical streaming standby in Docker. Writes go to the primary; reads are served from whichever node is authoritative at that instant, falling back to the primary when the standby lags. The filesystem is eventually consistent with the standby's lag continuously bounded by the freshness check, and a standby failure never causes data loss or a kernel-visible error.
  • Performance Optimizations: pgfs incorporates a structured performance optimization pipeline targeting database access latency, connection concurrency, userspace buffering, and FUSE kernel-transport tuning.
  • Kernel Offloading: pgfs incorporates Database-Native Kernel Offloading capabilities, utilizing copy_file_range, fallocate, reflink CoW, and server-side search to eliminate userspace byte streaming and deliver sub-millisecond execution for large-scale file operations.
  • Dual-Interface Architecture: pgfs features a Dual-Interface Storage Architecture providing a sub-100µs Local In-Process Engine (pgrx + zero SQL parsing + io_uring zero copy) and a scalable Remote Async Network Engine (tokio-postgres + pipelining).
  • Sharded Filesystem: A pgfs mount can be backed by N independent Postgres host nodes with RAID-5-like subset replication: each directory subtree is pinned to a replication set of R of the N hosts (never a full mirror on every host). Writes fan out to every member of the set; reads consult a quorum and return the newest version. Any number of clients can mount the same namespace from different machines and add files to one shared tree, and a host failure degrades reads and writes to the remaining healthy members without stale or corrupt data.

docs.title: Explanation: Atomic Rename
docs.text:
Status: Stable

File and directory renames, overwrite semantics and the full POSIX error matrix are implemented and covered by test_rename.sh and test_git_init.sh. renameat2 flags (RENAME_NOREPLACE, RENAME_EXCHANGE) are rejected.

Users can rename (move) files and directories with standard mv semantics, including overwriting existing files and empty directories.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Why rename has to be atomic
docs.text:
Rename is how Unix programs publish changes safely. An editor saves by writing a temporary file and renaming it over the original. Package managers install files the same way. Git guards every configuration change and every branch update with a lock file that is renamed into place. All of them rely on one guarantee: at every instant the target name refers to a complete file, either the old one or the new one.

A filesystem that implemented rename as "delete the target, then move the source" would open a window in which the name refers to nothing. A crash in that window loses the file. So rename was the first pgfs feature that had to be transactional rather than merely correct.

docs.title: One transaction, every row
docs.text:
In pgfs every entry stores the full path of its parent directory. Moving a file therefore changes one entries row and its blocks. Moving a directory changes every row beneath it, because every one of those rows has the old path baked in.

pgfs does all of it, including deleting an overwritten target, in a single PostgreSQL transaction. PostgreSQL then supplies the guarantees. Atomicity: after a crash the rename either happened completely or not at all. Isolation: any other connection sees the tree only before or after the move. The daemon's own in-memory inode map is updated only after the commit succeeds, so a failed rename leaves no trace.

docs.title: The price of materialised paths
docs.text: Rewriting every descendant makes the cost of a directory rename proportional to the size of its subtree. Renaming a directory holding a million files rewrites a million rows. Local filesystems avoid this by naming directories with inode numbers instead of paths, which makes a move a single pointer update. The schema already carries ino and parent_ino columns for exactly that change, described as InoBasedRekeyingReq in Performance Optimizations.

docs.title: Why git is the test
docs.text: git init exercises rename-overwrite immediately: it creates config, then rewrites it several times through config.lock. It was also the first real program run against pgfs, and it failed until directories were implemented. Git's workflow, made of lock files, renames and readers that expect complete files, is a compact stand-in for the guarantees real applications need, so test_git_init.sh is part of the integration suite.

docs.title: Why renameat2 flags are refused
docs.text:
RENAME_NOREPLACE and RENAME_EXCHANGE need their own atomic implementations: "fail if the target exists" and "swap two entries". Rather than approximate them, pgfs rejects them with EINVAL, which well-behaved tools such as GNU mv already handle by falling back to plain rename.

docs.title: Explanation: Dual-Interface Architecture
docs.text:
Status: Planned, not implemented

The PgfsBackend trait, its error mapping and an inode-keyed implementation on Db exist and are unit-tested, but the FUSE layer does not route through them yet. RemoteBackend is a stub, the pgrx engine and the io_uring transport are at the design stage, and there is no --backend option.

pgfs features a Dual-Interface Storage Architecture providing a sub-100µs Local In-Process Engine (pgrx + zero SQL parsing + io_uring zero copy) and a scalable Remote Async Network Engine (tokio-postgres + pipelining).

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Two very different places to run
docs.text:
pgfs is used in two settings with opposite constraints. On a single machine, the database is local and the dominant costs are the overheads around each query: building SQL text, parsing and planning it, and copying bytes between the kernel, the daemon and PostgreSQL. Over a network, a round-trip costs far more than any of that, and what matters is sending fewer of them: pipelining, batching and replicas.

One engine cannot be optimal for both. The dual-interface design gives each its own engine behind one interface.

docs.title: The local engine: no SQL on the hot path
docs.text: The planned local engine runs inside PostgreSQL itself, as a background worker written with pgrx. The FUSE daemon passes it compact binary requests over a shared-memory queue, and the worker executes pre-planned statements with binary parameters, so no SQL text is formatted, parsed or planned per operation. With io_uring buffer rings, file data could travel from the kernel into memory the worker reads directly, without intermediate copies. The target is operation latency under 100 µs.

docs.title: The remote engine: fewer round-trips
docs.text: The planned remote engine is an ordinary out-of-process client built on tokio-postgres. It pipelines queries over each connection, uses a connection pool, and reuses the replica freshness cache from Replicated Storage. It suits mounts where the database is on another host.

docs.title: Why a trait comes first
docs.text: Both engines need the FUSE layer to stop speaking SQL-shaped paths and start speaking inode-shaped operations. The PgfsBackend trait is that contract. It also forces the error model into the open: a backend reports NotFound or DatabaseError, and one place decides which errno the kernel sees. Building the trait and an inode-keyed implementation first, with tests, makes the eventual switch-over a mechanical change in fs.rs rather than a rewrite.

docs.title: What stands in the way
docs.text:
The running FUSE path stores data keyed by path, with 64 KiB blocks, and leaves the inode columns at their defaults. The backend implementation expects real inode links and uses 128 KiB blocks. Moving the FUSE layer onto the trait therefore also means migrating the schema (InoBasedRekeyingReq in Performance Optimizations) and settling on one block size.

docs.title: Explanation: Regular Files
docs.text:
Status: Stable

Create, read, write, append, truncate and delete are implemented and covered by unit and integration tests. Permissions, ownership and timestamps are reported but not settable (see Reference).

Users can create, read, write, and delete files through standard POSIX file operations on the mounted directory.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: A file is a handful of rows
docs.text:
pgfs stores each file as one row in entries, which holds its name, kind, size and modification time, plus zero or more rows in blocks, each holding up to 64 KiB of its contents. Both are keyed by the file's location: the path of the directory that contains it (parent) and its own name. A file at docs/sub/notes.txt is the row ('docs/sub', 'notes.txt').

Path-based keys make the tables readable by a person with psql. Ordinary SQL answers questions like "which files under docs/ changed today". The cost of path keys appears when a directory is renamed, which is discussed in Atomic Rename.

docs.title: Why blocks
docs.text:
The first version of pgfs stored a whole file in one bytea column; entries.data is the remnant. Every write then meant reading the whole file, changing a few bytes, and writing the whole file back. Appending a line to a 100 MB log rewrote 100 MB.

Fixed-size blocks bound that work. A write touches only the blocks it overlaps, and a read fetches only the blocks it covers. The block size is a trade-off. Smaller blocks mean less rewriting for small writes but more rows and more per-row overhead for large files. 64 KiB keeps the row count low while keeping a partial-block rewrite cheap. PostgreSQL compresses and moves values of that size out of line through TOAST on its own.

Blocks that were never written simply do not exist, so sparse files are free. A read fills the gaps with zeros, which is exactly what POSIX requires of a hole.

docs.title: Why writes are buffered per open file
docs.text:
The kernel delivers a large write to FUSE in pieces. Turning each piece into its own PostgreSQL transaction would make the commit round-trip, not the data, the bottleneck. pgfs instead collects writes in memory, per open file, as a set of dirty blocks, and commits them all in one transaction when the file is flushed, fsynced or closed.

This is close-to-open consistency, the model NFS uses. A writer and anything that opens the file after the writer closes it see the same bytes. Readers using the same mount see the data even sooner, because a read first flushes that file's pending writes.

docs.title: Durability is a deliberate trade
docs.text: pgfs turns off PostgreSQL's synchronous_commit. Commits return without waiting for the WAL to reach disk, which removes the largest fixed cost from every metadata operation. In exchange, a PostgreSQL crash can lose the last fraction of a second of acknowledged work. This is similar to how a local filesystem's page cache behaves without fsync, except that here even fsync does not close the gap. Transactions remain atomic: a lost commit disappears entirely and never leaves a half-written file. Performance Optimizations covers this and the other trade-offs in more depth.

docs.title: What the prototype does not model
docs.text:
pgfs reports fixed permissions (0644 for files) and the daemon's own uid and gid, and ignores chmod, chown and explicit timestamps. It has no symbolic or hard links. Inode numbers live only in memory. These are scoping decisions, not accidents. The schema already carries mode, uid, gid and a persistent ino column for the planned inode-keyed storage engine described in Dual-Interface Architecture.

docs.title: Explanation: Directory Trees
docs.text:
Status: Stable

mkdir, rmdir, readdir and nested paths of any depth are implemented and covered by test_dirs.sh. Directory timestamps are not tracked.

Users can create nested directories, list their contents, and remove empty directories through standard POSIX directory operations.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Directories are rows too
docs.text:
A directory is an entries row with kind = 'dir' and no blocks. What makes the tree a tree is the parent column: every row stores the full path of the directory that contains it. Listing a directory is a single indexed query, WHERE parent = 'project/src', and finding everything below a directory is a prefix match on that column.

This is the materialised-path pattern. Reading is easy: listings, subtree queries and path lookups are each one indexed query, and the rows are readable on their own. Moving things is harder, because a directory's path is copied into every descendant row, so renaming the directory rewrites them all. Atomic Rename explains how pgfs keeps that atomic, and Performance Optimizations describes the planned inode-keyed layout that would make it constant-time.

docs.title: The root
docs.text: The root has no parent, so it is stored as the row with an empty parent and an empty name, created together with the schema and pinned to inode 1, which FUSE requires. Its attributes are synthesised and never fetched, so the root can always be listed, even when the database is unreachable.

docs.title: What directories do not track
docs.text: On a local filesystem a directory's link count is two plus its number of subdirectories, and its modification time changes whenever an entry is added or removed. pgfs reports a fixed link count of 2 and the epoch as every timestamp. Tracking either would mean updating the parent's row on every create, delete and rename, adding a write to operations that are currently a single statement. Few programs depend on these values; tools that do (backup software comparing directory mtimes, for example) treat every pgfs directory as unchanged.

docs.title: Why rmdir refuses non-empty directories
docs.text:
POSIX requires it, and it is a safety feature. rm -r is the explicit way to delete a subtree, and it walks the tree bottom-up, removing each entry through the normal unlink and rmdir paths.

docs.title: Explanation: Kernel Offloading
docs.text:
Status: Partially implemented

Server-side copy_file_range and fallocate are implemented in the storage backend and unit-tested, but the FUSE layer does not call them yet. On a mount, copies stream through the daemon and fallocate fails with EOPNOTSUPP. Reflink, subtree clone and content search are planned.

pgfs incorporates Database-Native Kernel Offloading capabilities, utilizing copy_file_range, fallocate, reflink CoW, and server-side search to eliminate userspace byte streaming and deliver sub-millisecond execution for large-scale file operations.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Moving work to where the data is
docs.text:
In a normal copy, a program reads a file into its own memory and writes it back out. On pgfs, that means every byte travels from PostgreSQL to the daemon, up to the program through the kernel, back down through the kernel to the daemon, and into PostgreSQL again: four copies to produce data the database already has.

Linux provides calls that describe intent instead of moving bytes. copy_file_range means "make this range of that file appear here". fallocate means "reserve this space" or "this range is now empty". A filesystem that understands them can do the work where the data lives. For pgfs that is the query engine: a copy becomes one INSERT … SELECT over block rows, and punching a hole becomes one DELETE.

docs.title: The roadmap
docs.text: The same idea extends further. With reference-counted blocks, a reflink copy (cp --reflink) would copy only references, and blocks would be duplicated lazily on the first write. Cloning a whole directory tree could be one transaction of set-based inserts. Content search could use PostgreSQL's trigram indexes instead of reading every file through FUSE. Each of these is specified as a requirement; none is built yet.

docs.title: Why it is not wired in yet
docs.text: The offloading code is written against the inode-keyed storage interface, the future of pgfs storage. The mount still runs on the path-keyed layout. Exposing the callbacks before the FUSE layer moves to the new interface would mean implementing them twice, against two schemas and two block sizes. The Dual-Interface Architecture page describes that migration.

docs.title: Correctness before speed
docs.text:
Offloaded operations must be indistinguishable from the slow path: same bytes, same sizes, same holes. That is why the backend falls back to block-by-block copying whenever ranges are not block-aligned. A fast path that changed results would be worse than no fast path.

docs.title: Explanation: Observability & Diagnostics
docs.text:
Status: Stable

Tracing, the 60-second metrics, the SIGUSR1 state dump, error chains and crash reports all ship today. Of the per-errno counters, only eio and enoent are incremented yet.

Operators can see what the daemon is doing, how fast it is doing it, and why something failed, from the log alone: structured spans for every operation, periodic metrics, an on-demand state dump, and self-contained error chains and crash reports.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: The kernel only hears an errno
docs.text: When something fails inside a FUSE callback, the kernel can be told exactly one thing: an error number. EIO carries no message, no location and no cause. The process that called read learns that something went wrong and nothing else. Everything an operator needs to fix the problem therefore has to be in the daemon's own log, and pgfs is built around that.

docs.title: Errors that tell a story
docs.text:
Every fallible step in pgfs wraps its error with what it was trying to do and where, using #[track_caller] so the location is the caller's line, not the helper's. As an error travels up from the database driver through the storage layer to the FUSE callback, it accumulates a chain: "lookup during readdir, at this line, because fetching attributes, at that line, failed because the connection closed". The rule is that an operator should never need a debugger or the source code to understand a failure.

The other half of the rule is to not log what is normal. A shell probing for a file that does not exist is not an error, and logging every ENOENT would bury real failures. Expected conditions are answered with their errno and nothing else. Only unexpected failures are logged, always at ERROR and always with the full chain.

docs.title: Spans instead of log lines
docs.text: pgfs uses the tracing crate rather than plain logging. Each FUSE callback opens a span, and each database call opens a span inside it. Any message emitted underneath carries the full context, and timing tools can attribute time to "FUSE" versus "database". JSON output keeps the same structure for machines.

docs.title: Metrics that are cheap enough to keep on
docs.text: The counters are atomic integers and the histograms are seven atomic buckets, so recording costs a few nanoseconds and is always on. Fixed buckets and percentiles approximated to a bucket bound are coarse, but they answer the questions that matter in operation: is it a 100 µs filesystem or a 10 ms one, and is it getting worse. Separating eio from expected errnos lets an operator tell a spike in "file not found" from a spike in "database down". Exporting through the log keeps the first iteration free of extra endpoints; the counters are plain statics, so an exporter can be added without changing the instrumentation.

docs.title: Asking a running daemon
docs.text: SIGUSR1 requests a snapshot without restarting anything. Signal handlers are severely restricted in what they may do, so the signal only sets a flag. The next FUSE callback, which runs in a normal context, writes the dump. On an idle mount that means the dump waits for the next access, a deliberate trade for never doing real work inside signal handling.

docs.title: Crash reports
docs.text:
A panic report is written to both stderr and the log, because either may be the one an operator actually has. It includes the version, platform and compiler, so it can be pasted into a bug report as is.

docs.title: Explanation: On-Demand Profiling
docs.text:
Status: Stable

The SIGUSR2 CPU profiler, the Chrome span trace and scripts/bench_profile.sh ship today behind the profiling Cargo feature. Default builds contain none of it.

Operators can profile a running pgfs daemon without restarting it: SIGUSR2 starts and stops a CPU sampler that writes a flamegraph, and a span trace of every FUSE callback and database call is written on shutdown. All of it is compiled in only with the profiling feature.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Measuring instead of guessing
docs.text: pgfs sits between two systems that each have their own costs: the kernel's FUSE transport and PostgreSQL. When an operation is slow, the cause could be in either, or in the daemon in between, and intuition about which is unreliable. That is why profiling is a first-class, specified capability rather than an ad hoc perf record.

docs.title: Two views of the same run
docs.text: A sampling CPU profiler answers "where does the processor spend its time". In a database-backed filesystem much of the time is spent waiting on a socket for PostgreSQL, which barely shows up in a CPU profile. The span trace answers the other question, "where does the wall-clock time go", because every FUSE callback and every database call is a timed span with its parent recorded. Together they distinguish "the daemon is busy", "the daemon is waiting on the database" and "the kernel is sending too many small requests".

docs.title: On demand, on a running daemon
docs.text: Restarting a daemon to profile it changes the thing being measured: caches are cold and the workload is interrupted. SIGUSR2 lets an operator bracket exactly the interval of interest on a live process. The signal only flips state on the dedicated signal thread, and the profiler is started and stopped there, so profiling never runs inside a signal handler and never allocates on the FUSE dispatch path.

docs.title: Zero cost when off
docs.text: Sampling profilers install timers and signal handlers, and span recorders buffer every event. Neither belongs in a default build. Gating both behind a Cargo feature means a normal build contains no profiling instructions at all, not merely disabled ones. Metrics and tracing spans stay on in every build because they are cheap enough to leave running; see Observability.

docs.title: What the benchmark phases are for
docs.text:
Each phase of bench_profile.sh isolates one cost. Appending in 4 KiB writes exposes per-write overhead. A sequential read exposes per-block fetch cost. Creating thousands of empty files exposes per-operation round-trips with no data at all. A regression shows up in the phase whose cost it affects, and the matching flamegraph shows why.

docs.title: Explanation: Performance Optimizations
docs.text:
Status: Partially implemented

Chunked blocks, prepared statements, asynchronous commit, unlogged tables, per-handle write buffering, transaction batching and the attribute-cache TTL are implemented. Inode-keyed storage, the multi-threaded connection pool and the kernel writeback cache are not. The Reference page has the per-requirement status.

pgfs incorporates a structured performance optimization pipeline targeting database access latency, connection concurrency, userspace buffering, and FUSE kernel-transport tuning.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Where the time goes
docs.text: Every filesystem call on a pgfs mount crosses two boundaries. The kernel hands the request to the daemon through /dev/fuse, and the daemon turns it into one or more PostgreSQL queries over a socket. Each query pays for a round-trip, for parsing and planning (unless prepared), and at commit time for flushing the write-ahead log to disk. Optimising pgfs mostly means removing round-trips, removing parsing, and deciding how much durability each commit buys.

docs.title: Storage layout
docs.text: Storing files as 64 KiB blocks rather than one value per file bounds the cost of a small write to one block, not the whole file; see Regular Files. Keying rows by path keeps them readable but makes directory renames proportional to subtree size. The planned inode-keyed layout trades that readability for constant-time renames.

docs.title: Fewer, cheaper queries
docs.text: Prepared statements move parsing and planning to connection time. Wrapping multi-statement operations in one transaction replaces several commits, each with its own WAL flush, by one. Per-handle write buffering turns a stream of small writes into one transaction at close.

docs.title: Durability as a dial
docs.text: A commit normally waits until its WAL record is on disk, which on most storage is the slowest step of a small write. pgfs turns that wait off (synchronous_commit = off). Transactions stay atomic and the database stays consistent, but a PostgreSQL crash can lose the last fraction of a second of acknowledged commits. --unlogged goes further and skips WAL entirely. It is fastest, but a crash empties the tables, and unlogged tables do not replicate. Both are reasonable for development and caches. Neither is right for data that exists nowhere else.

docs.title: Letting the kernel answer
docs.text: Tools like ls -l, find and build systems ask for file attributes far more often than files change. With an attribute TTL, the kernel answers repeated questions from its own cache for that long, and pgfs never sees them. The price is staleness for changes made outside this mount, which is why the TTL is a flag rather than a constant.

docs.title: What is not done yet, and why
docs.text:
The connection pool exists, but FUSE dispatch in pgfs is single-threaded and the filesystem object is mutated through &mut self, so only one request is ever in flight. More connections would not help until dispatch is concurrent. The kernel's writeback cache would let the page cache merge small writes before they reach pgfs, but it changes when and how writes arrive (including writes from the kernel itself for pages it caches), so it has to wait for the write path to handle that correctly.

docs.title: Explanation: Project-Local Development Environment
docs.text:
Status: Stable

Everything on this page ships today: scripts/init_db.sh, scripts/pgfs.sh, the Makefile targets and the integration suite in scripts/test_*.sh.

A contributor goes from a fresh clone to a live pgfs mount with one command. The Postgres cluster, the mount point, the logs and the pid files all live under the project's testdata/ directory, so nothing touches a system-wide Postgres and rm -rf testdata is a full reset.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Why everything lives in testdata/
docs.text:
A filesystem backed by a database needs a database, and the usual way to get one is to install a system PostgreSQL service and administer it. pgfs deliberately avoids that. The cluster, its socket, its logs, the mount point and the daemon's bookkeeping all live in one git-ignored directory inside the checkout.

That buys three things. Nothing on the machine changes outside the project, so it is safe to experiment. Two checkouts never interfere with each other. And recovery from any mess is one command, rm -rf testdata, because there is no state anywhere else.

docs.title: Trust authentication, and its limits
docs.text:
The cluster uses trust authentication: any connection that reaches it is accepted without a password. The Unix socket sits in a directory only the developer can enter, so for socket connections that is no weaker than file permissions. The TCP listener is different. It only binds 127.0.0.1, but any user on the same machine can reach loopback. On a single-user development machine that is acceptable. On a shared host it is not, and the cluster should not be run there as is.

TCP exists at all because physical replication needs it: pg_basebackup and the standby's WAL receiver connect to the primary over the network (see Replicated Storage).

docs.title: Why a lifecycle script instead of raw commands
docs.text:
A FUSE mount has more states than "up" and "down". The daemon can be dead while the kernel still shows the mount. The mount can be busy because a shell has its working directory inside it. Postgres can be stopped while the daemon is starting. pgfs.sh treats /proc/mounts as the source of truth and escalates through progressively stronger actions (signal, then fusermount3 -u, then a lazy unmount), so the common failure states resolve themselves. The reasoning behind clean unmounts is covered in Reliable Mount.

pgfs.sh builds and runs the debug binary. Compiles are faster, and in debug builds a panic unwinds and prints a full report rather than aborting.

docs.title: Why the Makefile insists on the Nix shell
docs.text: pgfs links against libfuse and talks to a specific PostgreSQL major version. A build against the wrong libfuse headers, or an initdb from a different major version than the server, fails in confusing ways. The check-nix guard turns that into one clear message with a fix.

docs.title: Where the documentation comes from
docs.text:
These pages are generated. Every user-visible capability of pgfs is a Feature class in spec/ that inherits libspec.diataxis.Diataxis and must implement four methods, one per documentation quadrant. scripts/build_docs.py renders them, together with each feature's requirement classes, into this site. Documentation that lives next to the specification is reviewed in the same change as the behaviour it describes.

docs.title: Explanation: Reliable Mount & Shutdown
docs.text:
Status: Stable

AutoUnmount, signal-driven clean unmount, the deadlock watchdog, health files and the pgfs.sh escalation path are all implemented.

The filesystem mounts and unmounts cleanly. Crashing or killing the daemon never leaves a ghost mount behind.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: What a ghost mount is
docs.text: A FUSE filesystem is a contract between the kernel and a user process: the kernel forwards every operation on the mount to the process and waits for an answer. If the process disappears and nobody tells the kernel, the mount stays. Every access to it fails with "Transport endpoint is not connected", and tools that walk the filesystem tree, such as df, find / and backup jobs, hit the dead mount and stall or fail. That is a ghost mount, and avoiding them shaped how pgfs starts and stops.

docs.title: Three layers, weakest to strongest
docs.text:
The lifecycle script treats /proc/mounts as the source of truth rather than trusting PID files. If a mount exists with no live daemon behind it, pgfs.sh up sweeps it before mounting again. pgfs.sh down escalates from a polite signal to fusermount3 -u to a lazy unmount, and on the way it names the processes holding the mount busy, because "device busy" with no explanation is the most common frustration.

Signal handling turns the polite signals into a clean unmount. pgfs blocks the signals it cares about in every thread and receives them with sigwait on one dedicated thread. That thread can safely take locks and call the unmount routine, which an asynchronous signal handler cannot. The signals are blocked before anything else happens, so a Ctrl+C during startup is queued rather than killing a half-initialised daemon.

AutoUnmount is the layer that cannot fail. With it, the kernel itself watches the daemon process and removes the mount when the process exits for any reason: a clean return, a panic, SIGKILL or the OOM killer. Every other layer is a courtesy that produces a cleaner shutdown and clearer logs. AutoUnmount is the guarantee.

docs.title: Why release builds abort on panic
docs.text: A panic in a FUSE daemon usually means an invariant has broken. Unwinding can leave the process alive in an inconsistent state and still answering kernel requests. In release builds, pgfs aborts instead. The panic hook writes a crash report first, and AutoUnmount turns the abort into a clean disappearance.

docs.title: Why a deadlock unmounts the filesystem
docs.text: A wedged daemon is worse than a dead one. The kernel keeps waiting on it, and every process that touches the mount hangs in uninterruptible sleep. The liveness heartbeat detects this: a thread that cannot make progress stops advancing a counter, and the next request to arrive replies with an error and triggers an unmount. This converts a hang into an error, which processes can handle.

docs.title: Health files
docs.text:
Supervisors need a cheap way to ask "is it up yet?" without parsing logs. The PID file appears once the database is reachable, and the readiness file appears once the mount exists. Both are keyed by a hash of the mount point, so several pgfs mounts on one machine do not collide.

docs.title: Explanation: Replicated Storage
docs.text:
Status: Partially implemented

Write routing, lag detection, transparent fallback and the Docker standby work today. File contents (read) are still always served by the primary, and a standby that is unreachable when the daemon starts is dropped for the daemon's lifetime without a warning.

A pgfs mount can be backed by a primary Postgres and a physical streaming standby in Docker. Writes go to the primary; reads are served from whichever node is authoritative at that instant, falling back to the primary when the standby lags. The filesystem is eventually consistent with the standby's lag continuously bounded by the freshness check, and a standby failure never causes data loss or a kernel-visible error.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Why a physical standby
docs.text: PostgreSQL's physical streaming replication ships the primary's write-ahead log byte for byte, and the standby replays it. The standby is therefore an exact copy of the whole cluster: same tables, same rows, same schema, with no extra setup and no schema to keep in sync. That is why pgfs never initialises the schema on the standby. Nothing it could create would be different from what replication already delivers.

docs.title: Reads can go anywhere, decisions cannot
docs.text:
A standby is always slightly behind. Serving a stale directory listing is a small, recoverable inaccuracy. Making a write decision from stale data is a correctness bug. If create checked a stale standby for an existing file, it could decide the name was free when it was not.

So pgfs draws the line between answering and deciding. Pure metadata reads may use the standby. Every mutation, and every read whose result decides what a mutation does, goes to the primary. A lagging standby can therefore make the mount look briefly out of date, but it can never make it write the wrong thing.

docs.title: Measuring lag instead of assuming it
docs.text:
Before using the standby, pgfs compares two positions in the write-ahead log: how far the primary has written, and how far the standby has replayed. If the standby has replayed at least as far, it holds everything the primary holds, and reading from it is indistinguishable from reading the primary.

That check costs three small queries. Running it before every read would cost more than the reads it offloads, so the verdict is cached for half a second. This is the one place where pgfs trades strictness for speed. Inside that window, a read can see the standby's slightly older state.

docs.title: Failing towards availability
docs.text: When the standby is stale, unreachable or broken, pgfs reads from the primary and says so once per minute in the log. The programs using the mount never see an error. A replicated mount degrades into a single-node mount, which is still correct and only less scalable.

docs.title: What replication does not give you
docs.text: The standby offloads reads; it does not protect writes. If the primary fails, the mount fails. pgfs does not promote the standby or redirect writes, and a promoted standby is a new primary that pgfs would have to be restarted against. High availability for writes is a property of the PostgreSQL deployment underneath, not of pgfs.

docs.title: Why Docker, and why host networking
docs.text:
The standby needs its own PostgreSQL instance with its own data directory and port. A container provides that without a second installation, and the named volume survives container restarts. Host networking lets the container reach the primary on loopback, so the primary never has to listen on a routable interface.

docs.title: Explanation: Sharded Filesystem
docs.text:
Status: Planned, not implemented

Specified and designed (design/sharded_filesystem.md), not implemented. The daemon does not accept --shards or --replication-factor, and scripts/shard_db.sh does not exist yet. The tutorial and how-to describe the intended interface.

A pgfs mount can be backed by N independent Postgres host nodes with RAID-5-like subset replication: each directory subtree is pinned to a replication set of R of the N hosts (never a full mirror on every host). Writes fan out to every member of the set; reads consult a quorum and return the newest version. Any number of clients can mount the same namespace from different machines and add files to one shared tree, and a host failure degrades reads and writes to the remaining healthy members without stale or corrupt data.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: From one database to many
docs.text: Today a pgfs namespace lives in one PostgreSQL database, optionally with a read-only standby. That caps capacity at one machine's disk and makes that machine a single point of failure. The sharded design spreads the namespace across N independent hosts and lets many clients mount it at once.

docs.title: Why not mirror everything
docs.text: Copying every file to every host is simple, but it wastes capacity, since N hosts hold one host's worth of data, and every write costs N writes. Instead each file lives on R of the N hosts, its replication set. With R = 3 of N = 5, losing any two hosts still leaves every file at least one copy, and losing any one keeps every set writable (two of three is a quorum), while total capacity grows with the number of hosts. This is the sense in which the design is "RAID-5-like": partial redundancy spread across members, not a full mirror. Unlike RAID 5, it copies whole files rather than computing parity.

docs.title: Why place by top-level directory
docs.text: Placement uses the entry's top-level name, so everything under /docs lives on one set. Hashing each file separately would spread a directory's children across every host, and every ls would become a cluster-wide merge. Subtree-sticky placement keeps listings and most renames local to one set, at the cost of hot spots if one top-level directory is much larger than the rest.

docs.title: Why quorums and versions
docs.text:
The hosts in a set are independent databases with no replication between them, so they can disagree, for example after one missed a write while it was down. A write therefore counts as done only when a majority of the set has it, and every write carries a version number. A read asks a majority and keeps the highest version. Any two majorities overlap, so a read always sees the latest acknowledged write, even with a member down.

Versions combine a client identifier with a per-client counter, so they can be compared without synchronised clocks. The cost is last-writer-wins semantics when two clients write the same file at the same time.

docs.title: Why inode numbers encode the set
docs.text: Each host's database has its own sequence, so two hosts would hand out the same numbers. Putting the set id in the high bits and letting one member of each set allocate makes inode numbers unique across the cluster without coordination between sets.

docs.title: What the design leaves out
docs.text:
Cross-client cache coherence is bounded staleness via the attribute TTL, not a guarantee: two clients can briefly see different views. Changing the host list requires a migration. Both are deliberate v1 limits, and the roadmap addresses the first with leases in Phase 5.

docs.title: How-To: Atomic Rename
docs.text:
Status: Stable

File and directory renames, overwrite semantics and the full POSIX error matrix are implemented and covered by test_rename.sh and test_git_init.sh. renameat2 flags (RENAME_NOREPLACE, RENAME_EXCHANGE) are rejected.

Users can rename (move) files and directories with standard mv semantics, including overwriting existing files and empty directories.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Replace a file without exposing a partial write
docs.text:
Write to a temporary name in the same directory, close it, then rename:

generate-report > .report.tmp && mv .report.tmp report.txt

Readers see the old report.txt or the new one, never a mix. Close the temporary file before renaming it; see Reference for why.

docs.title: Move a directory tree
docs.text:
mv projects/2024 archive/2024

The whole subtree moves in one transaction, however many entries it contains. Large trees take time proportional to their size.

docs.title: Replace an empty directory with another directory
docs.text: mv -T staging live      # `live` must be empty

docs.title: Rename without overwriting
docs.text:
mv -n draft.txt final.txt

GNU mv -n first tries renameat2(RENAME_NOREPLACE). pgfs rejects that flag with EINVAL, and mv falls back to checking for the target itself. The result is correct but not atomic against a concurrent creator.

docs.title: Swap two entries
docs.text: mv --exchange (RENAME_EXCHANGE) is not supported and fails with Invalid argument. Use three renames through a temporary name.

docs.title: Check that a rename landed in the database
docs.text:
SELECT parent, name, kind FROM entries
WHERE parent = 'archive' AND name = '2024';

Generated from spec.app.AtomicRename by scripts/build_docs.py. Edit the specification, not this page.

docs.title: How-To: Dual-Interface Architecture
docs.text:
Status: Planned, not implemented

The PgfsBackend trait, its error mapping and an inode-keyed implementation on Db exist and are unit-tested, but the FUSE layer does not route through them yet. RemoteBackend is a stub, the pgrx engine and the io_uring transport are at the design stage, and there is no --backend option.

pgfs features a Dual-Interface Storage Architecture providing a sub-100µs Local In-Process Engine (pgrx + zero SQL parsing + io_uring zero copy) and a scalable Remote Async Network Engine (tokio-postgres + pipelining).

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Choose a backend at startup
docs.text: Not available yet. There is no --backend option; the daemon always uses the in-process Db client over libpq.

docs.title: Add an operation to the storage interface
docs.text:
1. Add an async fn to PgfsBackend in src/backend.rs. If not every backend can support it, give it a default body that returns StorageError::InvalidArgument, as copy_file_range and fallocate do.
  2. Implement it for Db in db::backend_impl (src/db.rs).
  3. Forward it in impl PgfsBackend for LocalBackend.
  4. Add a stub to RemoteBackend.
  5. Add a test next to tests_offload in src/db.rs.

docs.title: Report a storage failure with the right errno
docs.text: Return the matching StorageError variant and convert it with libc::c_int::from(err) when replying to the kernel. Use DatabaseError (→ EIO) only for failures that are not a normal answer, and log those with their full context.

docs.title: Run only the backend tests
docs.text: cargo test backend

docs.title: Follow the design
docs.text:
The full design, including the shared-memory protocol and the io_uring data path, is in design/dual_interface_architecture.md.

Generated from spec.optimize.DualInterfaceArchitecture by scripts/build_docs.py. Edit the specification, not this page.

docs.title: How-To: Regular Files
docs.text:
Status: Stable

Create, read, write, append, truncate and delete are implemented and covered by unit and integration tests. Permissions, ownership and timestamps are reported but not settable (see Reference).

Users can create, read, write, and delete files through standard POSIX file operations on the mounted directory.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

All paths below are inside a mounted pgfs filesystem.

docs.title: Create an empty file
docs.text: touch notes.txt

docs.title: Replace a file's contents
docs.text:
printf 'new contents\n' > notes.txt

To replace contents so that readers see either the old or the new version and never a partial one, write a temporary file and rename it over the target (see Atomic Rename):

printf 'new contents\n' > .notes.txt.tmp && mv .notes.txt.tmp notes.txt

docs.title: Append
docs.text: echo 'another line' >> notes.txt

docs.title: Overwrite bytes in the middle of a file
docs.text: printf 'XY' | dd of=notes.txt bs=1 seek=4 conv=notrunc

docs.title: Make written data visible outside the mount
docs.text: Writes are held in memory per open file and committed to PostgreSQL when the file is closed, flushed or fsynced. Processes reading through the same mount always see their own and each other's writes, because a read flushes pending writes first. A SQL client, or a second pgfs daemon on the same database, sees the data once the writer closes the file or calls fsync.

docs.title: Truncate or extend a file
docs.text:
truncate -s 0 notes.txt      # empty it
truncate -s 1M notes.txt     # extend with zeros

docs.title: Create a sparse file
docs.text:
truncate -s 1G sparse.img

Ranges that were never written have no block rows and read as zeros, so this costs one row in entries and nothing in blocks.

docs.title: Delete a file
docs.text: rm notes.txt

docs.title: Find a file's rows in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
A file at docs/sub/notes.txt has parent = 'docs/sub' and name = 'notes.txt':

SELECT kind, size, mtime FROM entries WHERE parent = 'docs/sub' AND name = 'notes.txt';
SELECT block_no, length(data) FROM blocks WHERE parent = 'docs/sub' AND name = 'notes.txt' ORDER BY block_no;

Files at the top of the mount have parent = ''.

docs.title: Diagnose an Input/output error
docs.text:
EIO means something unexpected failed, usually the database. The full error chain is in the daemon log:

grep ERROR testdata/pgfs.log | tail -5

Each entry names the operation, the source location and the root cause; see Observability.

Generated from spec.app.FlatFilesystem by scripts/build_docs.py. Edit the specification, not this page.

docs.title: How-To: Directory Trees
docs.text:
Status: Stable

mkdir, rmdir, readdir and nested paths of any depth are implemented and covered by test_dirs.sh. Directory timestamps are not tracked.

Users can create nested directories, list their contents, and remove empty directories through standard POSIX directory operations.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Create nested directories
docs.text: mkdir -p a/b/c

docs.title: List a directory, including hidden entries
docs.text: ls -la a

docs.title: Remove an empty directory
docs.text: rmdir a/b/c

docs.title: Remove a directory and everything in it
docs.text: rm -r a

docs.title: Find out why rmdir says "Directory not empty"
docs.text:
Hidden files count. List everything:

ls -A a/b

Or ask the database directly; the result is the full path of every child of a/b:

SELECT parent || '/' || name FROM entries WHERE parent = 'a/b';

docs.title: Count everything below a directory
docs.text:
SELECT kind, count(*) FROM entries
WHERE parent = 'a' OR starts_with(parent, 'a/')
GROUP BY kind;

Use starts_with rather than LIKE 'a/%'. In a LIKE pattern, _ and % in directory names act as wildcards.

docs.title: Find the largest directories by total file size
docs.text:
SELECT parent, sum(size) AS bytes, count(*) AS files
FROM entries WHERE kind = 'file'
GROUP BY parent ORDER BY bytes DESC LIMIT 10;

Generated from spec.app.HierarchicalDirectories by scripts/build_docs.py. Edit the specification, not this page.

docs.title: How-To: Kernel Offloading
docs.text:
Status: Partially implemented

Server-side copy_file_range and fallocate are implemented in the storage backend and unit-tested, but the FUSE layer does not call them yet. On a mount, copies stream through the daemon and fallocate fails with EOPNOTSUPP. Reflink, subtree clone and content search are planned.

pgfs incorporates Database-Native Kernel Offloading capabilities, utilizing copy_file_range, fallocate, reflink CoW, and server-side search to eliminate userspace byte streaming and deliver sub-millisecond execution for large-scale file operations.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Copy a file
docs.text: cp works and the copy is exact, but today every byte passes through the daemon. cp calls copy_file_range(2); pgfs does not implement the FUSE callback, so the kernel falls back to reading and writing.

docs.title: Copy a large file or tree faster today
docs.text:
Copy inside the database, as in the tutorial, while nothing is writing to the source:

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO entries (parent, name, kind, size)
  SELECT parent, 'copy.bin', kind, size FROM entries WHERE parent = 'dir' AND name = 'orig.bin';
INSERT INTO blocks (parent, name, block_no, data)
  SELECT parent, 'copy.bin', block_no, data FROM blocks WHERE parent = 'dir' AND name = 'orig.bin';
COMMIT;

The new file appears on the mount once the attribute cache expires (--attr-ttl, default 1 s).

docs.title: Preallocate or punch holes
docs.text: Not available on a mount: fallocate fails with Operation not supported. To make a file sparse, truncate it and rewrite the parts you need, or extend it with truncate -s, which never stores the new bytes.

docs.title: Clone with cp --reflink
docs.text: Not available: cp --reflink=always fails with Operation not supported. Plain cp (or cp --reflink=auto) works.

docs.title: Search file contents in the database
docs.text:
Not available as a filesystem interface. For text files you can query blocks directly:

SELECT DISTINCT parent || '/' || name FROM blocks
WHERE position(convert_to('needle', 'UTF8') in data) > 0;

This scans every block, and it misses matches that span a block boundary.

docs.title: How-To: Observability & Diagnostics
docs.text:
Status: Stable

Tracing, the 60-second metrics, the SIGUSR1 state dump, error chains and crash reports all ship today. Of the per-errno counters, only eio and enoent are incremented yet.

Operators can see what the daemon is doing, how fast it is doing it, and why something failed, from the log alone: structured spans for every operation, periodic metrics, an on-demand state dump, and self-contained error chains and crash reports.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Change the log level
docs.text:
RUST_LOG=pgfs=debug ./scripts/pgfs.sh run              # every DB query
RUST_LOG=pgfs::fs=debug,pgfs::db=info ./scripts/pgfs.sh run

The default is pgfs=info. The level is read at startup, so changing it requires a restart.

docs.title: Get JSON logs for a log pipeline
docs.text:
RUST_LOG_FORMAT=json ./target/debug/pgfs testdata/mnt 2> pgfs.jsonl
jq -c 'select(.level == "ERROR")' pgfs.jsonl

docs.title: Find out why an operation returned "Input/output error"
docs.text:
grep ' ERROR ' testdata/pgfs.log | tail -5

Read each line left to right: the FUSE span that failed, then each layer's context with its file:line, then the root cause after the last :.

docs.title: Recover from "Input/output error" on every operation
docs.text:
If every access fails and the log shows connection errors, the daemon's database connection is gone. pgfs does not reconnect. Make sure PostgreSQL is running, then restart the daemon:

./scripts/ensure_db.sh
./scripts/pgfs.sh down && ./scripts/pgfs.sh up

docs.title: Take a snapshot of a running daemon
docs.text:
kill -USR1 <pid>
ls <mountpoint> > /dev/null     # any access triggers the dump

docs.title: Extract metrics from the log
docs.text:
grep -o 'metrics|ops|.*' testdata/pgfs.log | tail -1
grep -o 'metrics|latency|.*' testdata/pgfs.log | tail -2

docs.title: Check that the daemon is alive from a script
docs.text: pid=$(cat /tmp/pgfs-<hash>.pid) && kill -0 "$pid" && test -e /tmp/pgfs-<hash>.ready

docs.title: Get a useful crash report
docs.text:
Run with RUST_BACKTRACE=1 (or full) so the report includes a symbolised backtrace. The report is printed to stderr and logged at ERROR, so it ends up in testdata/pgfs.log when the daemon was started by pgfs.sh.

Generated from spec.app.ObservableDaemon by scripts/build_docs.py. Edit the specification, not this page.

docs.title: How-To: On-Demand Profiling
docs.text:
Status: Stable

The SIGUSR2 CPU profiler, the Chrome span trace and scripts/bench_profile.sh ship today behind the profiling Cargo feature. Default builds contain none of it.

Operators can profile a running pgfs daemon without restarting it: SIGUSR2 starts and stops a CPU sampler that writes a flamegraph, and a span trace of every FUSE callback and database call is written on shutdown. All of it is compiled in only with the profiling feature.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Run the bundled benchmark under the profiler
docs.text:
./scripts/bench_profile.sh

The script builds a release binary with profiling, mounts it at testdata/mnt (unmounting anything already there), and runs three phases, each wrapped in its own SIGUSR2 start/stop:

Phase Workload write-ampl 16 MB appended in 4 KiB writes (dd oflag=append) seq-read sequential read of that file in 1 MiB reads many-files 2000 empty file creations

It lists the profiles it wrote and the relevant log lines.

docs.title: Profile a production daemon
docs.text:
The daemon must be built with --features profiling. Then:

kill -USR2 <pid>      # start sampling
# ... let the workload run ...
kill -USR2 <pid>      # stop and write /tmp/pgfs-profile-<ts>.svg

On a default build, SIGUSR2 logs CPU profiling not compiled in — rebuild with --features profiling and does nothing else.

docs.title: Separate database time from FUSE time
docs.text: Use the span trace rather than the flamegraph. A FUSE callback that waits on PostgreSQL shows a long db:: span inside it but little CPU. Stop the daemon cleanly (SIGTERM, SIGINT or SIGHUP) so the trace file is written; a killed daemon writes no trace.

docs.title: Compare two builds
docs.text: Run the same workload against each build, take one profile per run, and compare the metrics|latency lines in their logs. The p50/p95/p99 figures are bucketed (see Observability); use the span trace for exact durations.

docs.title: Check that profiling is compiled out
docs.text:
cargo build --release
nm -C target/release/pgfs | grep -c pprof     # prints 0

Generated from spec.perf.OnDemandProfiling by scripts/build_docs.py. Edit the specification, not this page.

docs.title: How-To: Performance Optimizations
docs.text:
Status: Partially implemented

Chunked blocks, prepared statements, asynchronous commit, unlogged tables, per-handle write buffering, transaction batching and the attribute-cache TTL are implemented. Inode-keyed storage, the multi-threaded connection pool and the kernel writeback cache are not. The Reference page has the per-requirement status.

pgfs incorporates a structured performance optimization pipeline targeting database access latency, connection concurrency, userspace buffering, and FUSE kernel-transport tuning.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Cut metadata round-trips
docs.text:
Raise the kernel's attribute and entry cache lifetime:

pgfs --attr-ttl 10 <mountpoint>

Changes made through this mount are always visible to it. Changes made by other writers (SQL, or another pgfs daemon on the same database) can take up to the TTL to appear. Use 0 when several writers share a database and must see each other immediately.

docs.title: Make a throwaway mount faster
docs.text:
Point pgfs at a new database and pass --unlogged:

createdb -h "$PWD/testdata" scratch
pgfs --conn "host=$PWD/testdata dbname=scratch" --unlogged <mountpoint>

--unlogged applies only when pgfs creates the tables. To convert existing tables, unmount and run:

ALTER TABLE entries SET UNLOGGED;
ALTER TABLE blocks SET UNLOGGED;

Unlogged tables are emptied after a PostgreSQL crash and are not replicated: do not combine them with --replica, whose standby would see empty tables.

docs.title: Write large files efficiently
docs.text: Write through one open file and close it once. Every write on an open handle is buffered, and closing commits all of it in one transaction. Opening, writing and closing in a loop pays for one transaction per iteration.

docs.title: Get full commit durability
docs.text: Not configurable. pgfs sets synchronous_commit = off on every connection it opens, which overrides the server's default.

docs.title: Measure the effect of a change
docs.text:
Compare fuse total from two SIGUSR1 state dumps around a workload (see the tutorial), or the metrics|latency lines, or run ./scripts/bench_profile.sh (see On-Demand Profiling).

Generated from spec.optimize.OptimizationRoadmap by scripts/build_docs.py. Edit the specification, not this page.

docs.title: How-To: Project-Local Development Environment
docs.text:
Status: Stable

Everything on this page ships today: scripts/init_db.sh, scripts/pgfs.sh, the Makefile targets and the integration suite in scripts/test_*.sh.

A contributor goes from a fresh clone to a live pgfs mount with one command. The Postgres cluster, the mount point, the logs and the pid files all live under the project's testdata/ directory, so nothing touches a system-wide Postgres and rm -rf testdata is a full reset.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Run the Rust unit tests
docs.text:
Inside the Nix shell:

make test

This starts the project-local cluster if it is down (scripts/ensure_db.sh) and then runs cargo test. Most tests in src/db.rs talk to the live database. Outside the Nix shell, make refuses to run (PGFS_ROOT is unset); run ./scripts/ensure_db.sh && cargo test instead.

docs.title: Run the integration suite
docs.text:
./scripts/pgfs.sh down        # the suite mounts testdata/mnt itself
make test-integration

Each scripts/test_*.sh prints PASS or FAIL. A failing test prints the tail of its log; the full output is in testdata/<test>.log. test_replica.sh needs Docker.

To run a single test:

bash scripts/test_rename.sh

docs.title: Run the daemon in the foreground
docs.text:
RUST_LOG=pgfs=debug ./scripts/pgfs.sh run

Logs go to the terminal. Ctrl+C unmounts cleanly.

docs.title: Mount somewhere other than testdata/mnt
docs.text:
PGFS_MOUNT=/tmp/pgfs-demo ./scripts/pgfs.sh up
PGFS_MOUNT=/tmp/pgfs-demo ./scripts/pgfs.sh down

Pass the same PGFS_MOUNT to every pgfs.sh command.

docs.title: Use a PostgreSQL server other than the project-local one
docs.text:
Run the binary directly and give it a libpq connection string:

cargo build
./target/debug/pgfs --conn "host=db.internal port=5432 dbname=pgfs user=alice" /mnt/pgfs

The role needs permission to create tables in that database the first time; pgfs creates its schema on startup.

docs.title: Inspect the database directly
docs.text: psql -h "$PWD/testdata" -d pgfs

docs.title: Stop PostgreSQL
docs.text:
./scripts/pgfs.sh down
make db-stop

Unmount first. A running daemon does not reconnect after PostgreSQL comes back, so every operation fails with Input/output error until the daemon is restarted.

docs.title: Reset everything
docs.text:
./scripts/pgfs.sh down
make db-stop
rm -rf testdata

The next ./scripts/pgfs.sh up creates a fresh cluster.

docs.title: How-To: Reliable Mount & Shutdown
docs.text:
Status: Stable

AutoUnmount, signal-driven clean unmount, the deadlock watchdog, health files and the pgfs.sh escalation path are all implemented.

The filesystem mounts and unmounts cleanly. Crashing or killing the daemon never leaves a ghost mount behind.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Stop the daemon cleanly
docs.text:
./scripts/pgfs.sh down

Or signal it directly; SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGHUP all unmount cleanly:

kill -TERM "$(cat testdata/pgfs.pid)"

docs.title: Wait for the mount to be ready (supervisors, scripts)
docs.text:
Poll for the readiness file. Its name is printed at startup next to the PID file:

until [ -e /tmp/pgfs-<hash>.ready ]; do sleep 0.1; done

Or poll /proc/mounts for the mount point, which is what pgfs.sh up does.

docs.title: Fix "Device or resource busy" on unmount
docs.text:
A process has its working directory or an open file inside the mount. pgfs.sh down lists the holders and then lazy-unmounts. To find them yourself:

fuser -vm testdata/mnt

docs.title: Fix "Transport endpoint is not connected"
docs.text:
The daemon died and the mount was not removed, which happens only if it was started without AutoUnmount (see the user_allow_other warning below). Sweep it:

./scripts/pgfs.sh down

or fusermount3 -u -z testdata/mnt.

docs.title: Make AutoUnmount available
docs.text:
If the log shows mount with AutoUnmount failed (...); retrying without AutoUnmount, enable user_allow_other:

sudo sed -i 's/^#user_allow_other/user_allow_other/' /etc/fuse.conf

docs.title: Run pgfs under systemd
docs.text:
Use Type=simple, start the binary directly with an explicit --conn, and let systemd stop it with SIGTERM:

[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=/opt/pgfs/pgfs --conn "host=/run/postgresql dbname=pgfs" /srv/pgfs
KillSignal=SIGTERM
Restart=on-failure

Services that need the mount should wait for the .ready file, or for the mount point to appear in /proc/mounts.

docs.title: How-To: Replicated Storage
docs.text:
Status: Partially implemented

Write routing, lag detection, transparent fallback and the Docker standby work today. File contents (read) are still always served by the primary, and a standby that is unreachable when the daemon starts is dropped for the daemon's lifetime without a warning.

A pgfs mount can be backed by a primary Postgres and a physical streaming standby in Docker. Writes go to the primary; reads are served from whichever node is authoritative at that instant, falling back to the primary when the standby lags. The filesystem is eventually consistent with the standby's lag continuously bounded by the freshness check, and a standby failure never causes data loss or a kernel-visible error.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Provision the Docker standby
docs.text:
./scripts/replica_db.sh up
./scripts/replica_db.sh conn      # prints the --replica string

up restarts the primary with a loopback TCP listener if it does not already have one.

docs.title: Mount with a replica
docs.text:
./target/debug/pgfs --replica "$(./scripts/replica_db.sh conn)" testdata/mnt

scripts/pgfs.sh does not pass --replica; start the binary directly.

docs.title: Use a standby you manage yourself
docs.text:
Any physical streaming standby of the primary's database works:

pgfs --conn "host=primary.internal dbname=pgfs" \
     --replica "host=standby.internal dbname=pgfs" /srv/pgfs

pgfs never creates or alters the schema on the standby. It must be a physical copy of the primary.

docs.title: Check that the standby is healthy
docs.text:
./scripts/replica_db.sh status

Look for in recovery: t and a small replay_lag. Then ask the daemon what it thinks:

kill -USR1 <pid>; ls <mountpoint> > /dev/null
grep 'state|ino_cache' <daemon log> | tail -1     # replica fresh | stale or unreachable | none

docs.title: Tell whether reads are actually reaching the standby
docs.text:
Compare the counters in the minute-by-minute metrics line:

grep 'metrics|replica' <daemon log> | tail -3

reads growing means the standby is serving. fallbacks growing much faster means it is lagging or unreachable.

docs.title: Fix a standby that never catches up
docs.text:
Symptom: status shows in recovery: t, the daemon reports stale or unreachable, and the container log contains requested WAL segment ... has already been removed:

docker logs --tail 5 pgfs-replica

The primary has recycled WAL the standby still needs, usually because the standby was down for a long time. Rebuild it from a fresh base backup:

./scripts/replica_db.sh wipe
docker rm pgfs-replica 2>/dev/null    # if a stopped container remains
./scripts/replica_db.sh up

docs.title: Fix "container name /pgfs-replica is already in use"
docs.text:
A stopped container from an earlier run remains, and down only removes running containers:

docker rm pgfs-replica
./scripts/replica_db.sh up

docs.title: Attach a standby to a daemon that is already running
docs.text: Restart the daemon with --replica. The standby connection is made only at startup, and a standby that was unreachable then stays detached until the next restart.

docs.title: Remove the standby
docs.text:
./scripts/replica_db.sh down     # stop, keep data
./scripts/replica_db.sh wipe     # stop and delete the data volume

docs.title: How-To: Sharded Filesystem
docs.text:
Status: Planned, not implemented

Specified and designed (design/sharded_filesystem.md), not implemented. The daemon does not accept --shards or --replication-factor, and scripts/shard_db.sh does not exist yet. The tutorial and how-to describe the intended interface.

A pgfs mount can be backed by N independent Postgres host nodes with RAID-5-like subset replication: each directory subtree is pinned to a replication set of R of the N hosts (never a full mirror on every host). Writes fan out to every member of the set; reads consult a quorum and return the newest version. Any number of clients can mount the same namespace from different machines and add files to one shared tree, and a host failure degrades reads and writes to the remaining healthy members without stale or corrupt data.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

Planned interface

These instructions describe the designed interface. None of it is implemented yet.

docs.title: Deploy a sharded namespace
docs.text:
1. Run one PostgreSQL instance per host and create a pgfs database on each.
  2. Start pgfs on every client with the same host list and replication factor:
pgfs --shards "host=h1 dbname=pgfs,host=h2 dbname=pgfs,host=h3 dbname=pgfs,host=h4 dbname=pgfs,host=h5 dbname=pgfs" \
     --replication-factor 3 /srv/pgfs

Every client must list the hosts in the same order; placement is computed from the list.

docs.title: Choose N and R
docs.text: Use R = 3 and N ≥ R + 1. A file survives the loss of R − 1 members of its set and stays writable while a quorum (⌊R/2⌋ + 1) is up.

docs.title: Bound how stale other clients' changes can look
docs.text:
pgfs --shards "…" --attr-ttl 1 /srv/pgfs

Changes from other clients appear within the TTL.

docs.title: Detect a failing host
docs.text: Watch SHARD_DEGRADED_HOSTS and SHARD_QUORUM_MISSES in the minute-by-minute metrics, and use the SIGUSR1 state dump for per-host health.

docs.title: Recover a host
docs.text: Restart its PostgreSQL. On recovery the host is compared with the highest version of each entry in its sets and missing mutations are re-applied.

docs.title: Add or remove hosts
docs.text:
Not supported online. The topology is fixed at mount time, and changing it requires a migration run (design §3.4).

docs.title: Reference: Atomic Rename
docs.text:
Status: Stable

File and directory renames, overwrite semantics and the full POSIX error matrix are implemented and covered by test_rename.sh and test_git_init.sh. renameat2 flags (RENAME_NOREPLACE, RENAME_EXCHANGE) are rejected.

Users can rename (move) files and directories with standard mv semantics, including overwriting existing files and empty directories.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Outcome matrix
docs.text: Source Target Result file absent moved file file target atomically replaced file directory EISDIR directory absent moved with all descendants directory empty directory target atomically replaced directory non-empty directory ENOTEMPTY directory file ENOTDIR directory inside its own subtree EINVAL any itself success, no change absent any ENOENT any, with renameat2 flags ≠ 0 any EINVAL

docs.title: Transaction
docs.text:
Every check that decides the outcome reads the primary database, never a replica. A successful rename is one transaction:

  1. If the target exists, delete its entries row and its blocks rows.
  2. If the source is a directory, rewrite parent in every entries and blocks row below it, replacing the old path prefix with the new one.
  3. Update the source's entries row to the new (parent, name) and set its mtime.
  4. Move the source's blocks rows to the new (parent, name).
  5. Commit. If no row moved, roll back and reply EIO.

After the commit, the in-memory path ↔ inode maps are re-keyed for the entry and its whole subtree, so inode numbers the kernel already holds stay valid.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text: Rename Rows written file 1 entry + its blocks directory 1 entry + every descendant entry + every descendant block

docs.title: Open files
docs.text: Pending writes in an open file's buffer are tied to the path the file had when it was opened. Close or fsync a file before renaming it, otherwise those writes are not carried over to the new name.

docs.title: Isolation
docs.text: Concurrent SQL readers, and other pgfs daemons on the same database, see the tree either entirely before or entirely after the rename (PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED).

docs.title: Specification requirements
docs.text:
AtomicRename is built from these requirement classes. Each is declared in spec/ and listed in the feature's deps.

RenamesEntries

spec.app.RenamesEntries

A FUSE rename moves an entry from one (parent, name) to another. It follows POSIX semantics:

  • If the target exists and is a file, it is atomically replaced.
  • If the target exists and is an empty directory, it is atomically replaced.
  • If the target is a non-empty directory, the kernel receives ENOTEMPTY.
  • If source is a file and target is a directory, the kernel receives EISDIR.
  • If source is a directory and target is a file, the kernel receives ENOTDIR.
  • Renaming a directory cascades: every descendant's parent path is rewritten in the same database transaction.
  • The in-memory inode<->path maps are re-keyed for the entire subtree.
RejectsInvalidRenames

spec.app.RejectsInvalidRenames

A FUSE rename with non-zero flags replies EINVAL. Renaming a directory into one of its own descendants replies EINVAL. Renaming an entry onto itself is a no-op.

SupportsGitInit

spec.app.SupportsGitInit

Running git init inside the mounted filesystem succeeds without errors. This exercises the full rename-overwrite path: git creates .git/config, then uses lock+rename to set config values, which triggers rename-overwrite with POSIX semantics.

docs.title: Reference: Dual-Interface Architecture
docs.text:
Status: Planned, not implemented

The PgfsBackend trait, its error mapping and an inode-keyed implementation on Db exist and are unit-tested, but the FUSE layer does not route through them yet. RemoteBackend is a stub, the pgrx engine and the io_uring transport are at the design stage, and there is no --backend option.

pgfs features a Dual-Interface Storage Architecture providing a sub-100µs Local In-Process Engine (pgrx + zero SQL parsing + io_uring zero copy) and a scalable Remote Async Network Engine (tokio-postgres + pipelining).

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Component status
docs.text: Component Status Location PgfsBackend trait implemented, not used by the FUSE layer src/backend.rs StorageError → errno mapping implemented src/backend.rs inode-keyed implementation on Db implemented; exercised by unit tests only src/db.rs, backend_impl LocalBackend wrapper that forwards to Db; not the planned pgrx engine src/backend.rs RemoteBackend stub; every method returns an error src/backend.rs pgrx background-worker engine (LocalPgrxEngineReq) planned design only io_uring buffer rings (IoUringBufferRingReq) planned design only tokio-postgres network engine (RemoteAsyncBackendReq) planned design only --backend command-line option planned

docs.title: StorageError
docs.text: Variant errno NotFound ENOENT AlreadyExists EEXIST NotEmpty ENOTEMPTY InvalidArgument(String) EINVAL DatabaseError(String) EIO IoError(kind) ENOENT, EEXIST, EACCES or EINVAL for the matching kinds; otherwise EIO

docs.text: Type Fields FileKind File, Directory, Symlink FileAttr ino, size, blocks, atime, mtime, ctime, kind, perm, nlink, uid, gid, rdev, flags DirEntry ino, name, kind SetAttrInput optional mode, uid, gid, size, atime, mtime

docs.title: Compatibility with the running FUSE path
docs.text:
Property FUSE path (Db path methods) Backend path (Db as PgfsBackend) Key (parent, name) text ino, parent_ino integers Block size 65 536 bytes 131 072 bytes entries.parent_ino written always 1 the real parent blocks.ino written always 1 the real inode

Rows written by one path are not correctly visible through the other, so the two cannot yet serve the same database.

docs.title: Specification requirements
docs.text:
DualInterfaceArchitecture is built from these requirement classes. Each is declared in spec/ and listed in the feature's deps.

PgfsBackendTraitReq

spec.optimize.PgfsBackendTraitReq

A unified async PgfsBackend trait decouples the FUSE driver (src/fs.rs) from storage engine implementations.

Technical Details:

  • Exposes async methods: lookup, getattr, setattr, readdir, mkdir, rmdir, create, unlink, rename, read_block, write_block, truncate_blocks.
  • Maps database failures into structured StorageError variants (NotFound, AlreadyExists, NotEmpty, InvalidArgument, DatabaseError, IoError).
  • Enables pluggable backend switching (LocalBackend vs RemoteBackend) at daemon startup.
LocalPgrxEngineReq

spec.optimize.LocalPgrxEngineReq

The local storage engine (LocalBackend) operates inside PostgreSQL as a pgrx background worker (pg_bgworker) using pre-compiled SPI plans and binary Datums to achieve Zero SQL Text Parsing on the hot path.

Technical Details:

  • Runs inside PostgreSQL postmaster via RegisterBackgroundWorker.
  • Pre-compiles statement handles (SPIPlanPtr) during worker startup using SPI_prepare.
  • Receives binary operation descriptors over a lockless shared-memory ring buffer (shm_mq) from the standalone FUSE daemon.
  • Executes SPI_execute_plan using raw binary Datum values (Int64GetDatum, Int32GetDatum), bypassing SQL text formatting, parsing, and planning entirely.
IoUringBufferRingReq

spec.optimize.IoUringBufferRingReq

Where supported by kernel (Linux 6.9+ fuse-io_uring), pgfs utilizes io_uring Submission/Completion queues paired with pre-registered shared memory buffer rings (IORING_OP_PROVIDE_BUFFERS) for zero-copy data flow.

Technical Details:

  • Replaces /dev/fuse read()/write() syscalls with asynchronous io_uring SQ/CQ rings.
  • Maps POSIX shared memory buffers (shm_mq) as pre-registered io_uring buffer rings.
  • Kernel VFS places incoming file block payloads directly into shared memory buffers accessible by the pgrx worker, enabling end-to-end zero-copy data flow into PostgreSQL SharedBuffers.
RemoteAsyncBackendReq

spec.optimize.RemoteAsyncBackendReq

The remote storage engine (RemoteBackend) operates out-of-process using fuse3 and tokio-postgres over TCP or Unix sockets.

Technical Details:

  • Uses fuse3 async FUSE bindings and tokio-postgres connection pools (bb8).
  • Implements query pipelining over single connection handles using query_raw.
  • Integrates atomic ReplicaFreshnessCache for read-replica traffic routing.
