docs.title: Reference: Regular Files
docs.text:
Status: Stable

Create, read, write, append, truncate and delete are implemented and covered by unit and integration tests. Permissions, ownership and timestamps are reported but not settable (see Reference).

Users can create, read, write, and delete files through standard POSIX file operations on the mounted directory.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: FUSE operations
docs.text: Operation Triggered by Behaviour Errors lookup path resolution reads the entry's attributes; assigns an inode number on first sight ENOENT (absent, or name not valid UTF-8) getattr stat, ls -l reads attributes; the root (inode 1) is synthesised ENOENT create open(O_CREAT) checks the primary for an existing entry, inserts a file row with size 0, opens a write handle EEXIST open open allocates a handle with an empty dirty-block buffer; flags and permissions are not checked ENOENT read read, pread flushes the handle's pending writes, then fetches only the blocks covering the range; the range is clamped to the file size; holes read as zeros ENOENT write write, pwrite with an open handle, buffers the bytes in memory and returns immediately; without one, writes the touched blocks in one transaction; extends the size if the write ends past it ENOENT flush, fsync, release close, fsync writes the handle's dirty blocks and new size in one transaction EIO setattr truncate, ftruncate, open(O_TRUNC) size changes truncate or extend in one transaction; mode, owner and time changes are accepted and ignored EISDIR (size change on a directory), ENOENT unlink rm deletes the entry row, then its block rows; forgets the inode mapping EIO

docs.title: Storage schema
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE entries (
    ino        bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    parent_ino bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    parent     text   NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    name       text   NOT NULL,
    kind       text   NOT NULL DEFAULT 'file',   -- 'file' | 'dir'
    data       bytea  NOT NULL DEFAULT '',       -- legacy, always empty
    size       bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    mode       integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 33188,
    uid        integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1000,
    gid        integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1000,
    atime      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    mtime      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    ctime      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    CONSTRAINT unique_parent_name UNIQUE (parent, name)
);

CREATE TABLE blocks (
    ino      bigint  NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    parent   text    NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    name     text    NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    block_no integer NOT NULL,
    data     bytea   NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (parent, name, block_no)
);

Indexes: entries(parent_ino), entries(parent), blocks(ino, block_no). The schema is created on first connect with CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, inside one transaction that also inserts the root row (ino = 1, parent = '', name = '', kind = 'dir').

Property Value Block size 65 536 bytes (BLOCK_SIZE) Block number offset / 65536 Last block may be shorter than 65 536 bytes Holes blocks with no row; read as zeros Source of truth for size entries.size entries.ino, parent_ino, mode, uid, gid, atime, ctime written with defaults; not read by the FUSE path

docs.title: Reported attributes
docs.text:
Attribute Regular file perm 0644 nlink 1 uid, gid the daemon's own uid and gid size entries.size blocks ceil(size / 512) blksize 4096 atime, mtime, ctime, crtime all equal to entries.mtime

Attribute and entry replies carry the TTL set by --attr-ttl (default 1 s).

docs.title: Inode numbers
docs.text: Inode numbers are assigned in memory, per mount, the first time the kernel sees a path. They start at 2, increase by one, are never reused within a mount, and survive renames. They are not persisted: a remount assigns new numbers. They are unrelated to entries.ino.

docs.title: Durability
docs.text: Every connection runs SET synchronous_commit = off. A transaction is acknowledged once it is in PostgreSQL's WAL buffers, before the WAL is flushed to disk. fsync on a pgfs file waits for the commit, not for the disk flush. If PostgreSQL crashes, the most recently acknowledged commits can be lost; with default settings that window is under one second. Committed data is never partially applied. Buffered writes that have not reached flush, fsync or close are lost if the daemon dies.

docs.title: Error mapping
docs.text: errno Meaning ENOENT the entry, or the inode's path, does not exist EEXIST O_CREAT|O_EXCL on an existing name EISDIR size change requested on a directory EIO unexpected failure (database error, invariant violation); the full error chain is logged at ERROR

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text: Operation Result symbolic links (symlink) EPERM from ln -s (operation not implemented) hard links (link) EPERM from ln (operation not implemented) FIFOs, sockets, device nodes (mknod) ENOSYS extended attributes not implemented chmod, chown, utimes, touch -d succeed but have no effect statfs (df) reports zero size and zero free space fallocate EOPNOTSUPP (see Kernel Offloading) reflink clone (cp --reflink=always) EOPNOTSUPP

docs.title: Specification requirements
docs.text:
FlatFilesystem is built from these requirement classes. Each is declared in spec/ and listed in the feature's deps.

ConnectsToPostgres

spec.app.ConnectsToPostgres

The daemon connects to a Postgres database via a libpq connection string. On first connect it creates the entries table (ino, parent_ino, parent, name, kind, size, mode, uid, gid, atime, mtime, ctime) and blocks table (ino, parent, name, block_no, data) if they do not already exist. Connection failure produces a full error story including the connection string and the root cause.

CreatesFiles

spec.app.CreatesFiles

A FUSE create (O_CREAT) inserts a row with kind='file', empty data, size=0, and the current timestamp. If the entry already exists the kernel receives EEXIST. The reply includes a valid inode and file attributes with 0644 permissions.

ReadsFiles

spec.app.ReadsFiles

A FUSE read on a regular-file inode returns the byte range from the file's stored block chunks. Offset and size are clamped to the stored file length. Missing inodes reply ENOENT.

WritesFiles

spec.app.WritesFiles

A FUSE write updates touched block chunks or buffers dirty blocks per open file handle, persisting them to PostgreSQL. The write extends the file if the offset+length exceeds the current size.

TruncatesFiles

spec.app.TruncatesFiles

A FUSE setattr with a size parameter truncates or extends a regular file to the given size (zero-filled extension, deleting trailing block chunks in PostgreSQL). Size changes on directories reply EISDIR.

UnlinksFiles

spec.app.UnlinksFiles

A FUSE unlink deletes the row and removes the inode from the in-memory path map.

LooksUpEntries

spec.app.LooksUpEntries

A FUSE lookup on a (parent inode, name) pair returns the entry's inode and attributes, or ENOENT if absent. Lookup allocates a stable inode number for the entry's full path.

ReportsAttributes

spec.app.ReportsAttributes

A FUSE getattr returns size, kind, permissions, timestamps, and nlink for any inode. The root inode (ino=1) is always a directory.

DistinguishesExpectedErrors

spec.app.DistinguishesExpectedErrors

Expected conditions (ENOENT, EEXIST, ENOTEMPTY, EISDIR, ENOTDIR, EINVAL) are replied directly to the kernel without logging. Unexpected failures (database errors, invariant violations) are logged in full via log_and_reply! with the complete error chain and replied as EIO.

docs.title: Reference: Directory Trees
docs.text:
Status: Stable

mkdir, rmdir, readdir and nested paths of any depth are implemented and covered by test_dirs.sh. Directory timestamps are not tracked.

Users can create nested directories, list their contents, and remove empty directories through standard POSIX directory operations.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: FUSE operations
docs.text:
Operation Behaviour Errors mkdir checks the primary for an existing entry, then inserts a dir row EEXIST, ENOENT (parent unknown), EIO rmdir checks the primary that the entry exists, then that no row has it as parent, then deletes it ENOENT, ENOTEMPTY, EIO readdir returns ., .., then every child ordered by name ENOENT, EIO lookup resolves (parent inode, name) to attributes ENOENT

The emptiness check and the delete in rmdir are separate statements, not one transaction.

docs.title: readdir offsets
docs.text: Entries are numbered from 1 in the order returned: . is 1, .. is 2, and children follow sorted by name. The kernel resumes a partial listing by passing back the last number it received. Offsets index the current list, so if the directory changes between two calls of one listing, entries can be skipped or repeated.

docs.title: Directory attributes
docs.text: Attribute Value perm 0755 nlink 2, regardless of the number of subdirectories size, blocks 0 uid, gid the daemon's own uid and gid atime, mtime, ctime, crtime the Unix epoch (shown as 1970-01-01, or 1969-12-31 west of UTC)

docs.title: Root directory
docs.text: Property Value Inode 1 Path '' (empty string) Row parent = '', name = '', kind = 'dir', inserted at schema creation Attributes always synthesised; never read from the database Listing excludes the root's own row

docs.title: Paths and names
docs.text: Rule Detail Key (parent, name), unique Full path parent || '/' || name, or name when parent = '' Valid names any UTF-8 string without / or NUL; non-UTF-8 names are rejected with ENOENT Depth not limited by pgfs. The unique index on (parent, name) limits one key to about 2.7 kB, so a longer combined path fails with EIO. Index used by listings entries(parent)

docs.title: Specification requirements
docs.text:
HierarchicalDirectories is built from these requirement classes. Each is declared in spec/ and listed in the feature's deps.

CreatesDirectories

spec.app.CreatesDirectories

A FUSE mkdir inserts a row with kind='dir'. If the entry exists the kernel receives EEXIST. The reply includes a directory inode with 0755 permissions and nlink=2.

RemovesDirectories

spec.app.RemovesDirectories

A FUSE rmdir deletes the directory row only if the directory is empty (no child rows with matching parent path). If children exist the kernel receives ENOTEMPTY. If the entry does not exist the kernel receives ENOENT.

ListsDirectories

spec.app.ListsDirectories

A FUSE readdir returns '.' and '..' followed by every child of the directory inode, each with the correct inode number and file type. Offsets are synthetic (1-based index); the reply stops when the kernel's buffer is full and resumes on the next call.

LooksUpEntries

spec.app.LooksUpEntries

A FUSE lookup on a (parent inode, name) pair returns the entry's inode and attributes, or ENOENT if absent. Lookup allocates a stable inode number for the entry's full path.

ReportsAttributes

spec.app.ReportsAttributes

A FUSE getattr returns size, kind, permissions, timestamps, and nlink for any inode. The root inode (ino=1) is always a directory.

docs.title: Reference: Kernel Offloading
docs.text:
Status: Partially implemented

Server-side copy_file_range and fallocate are implemented in the storage backend and unit-tested, but the FUSE layer does not call them yet. On a mount, copies stream through the daemon and fallocate fails with EOPNOTSUPP. Reflink, subtree clone and content search are planned.

pgfs incorporates Database-Native Kernel Offloading capabilities, utilizing copy_file_range, fallocate, reflink CoW, and server-side search to eliminate userspace byte streaming and deliver sub-millisecond execution for large-scale file operations.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Requirement status
docs.text: Requirement Status Behaviour on a mount today CopyFileRangeReq backend only (Db as PgfsBackend) copy_file_range is not a FUSE callback in pgfs; the kernel falls back to read/write FallocatePunchHoleReq backend only fallocate replies EOPNOTSUPP ReflinkBlockSharingReq planned cp --reflink=always fails with EOPNOTSUPP CloneSubtreeReq planned not available ContentSearchOffloadReq planned not available

docs.title: Backend copy_file_range
docs.text:
copy_file_range(ino_in, off_in, ino_out, off_out, len) -> u64

Case Behaviour len == 0 returns 0 off_in, off_out and len all multiples of 131 072 one INSERT INTO blocks … SELECT … FROM blocks WHERE ino = ino_in with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, then UPDATE entries SET size = GREATEST(size, off_out + len), mtime = now(); returns len otherwise block-by-block read_block / write_block; returns bytes copied; source blocks with no row are skipped

The two statements of the aligned path are not wrapped in one transaction.

docs.title: Backend fallocate
docs.text:
fallocate(ino, offset, length, mode)

mode bits Behaviour FALLOC_FL_PUNCH_HOLE (0x02) DELETE FROM blocks WHERE ino = $1 AND block_no BETWEEN first AND last, covering every 128 KiB block the range touches, including partially covered ones without FALLOC_FL_KEEP_SIZE (0x01) size = GREATEST(size, offset + length); no blocks are written FALLOC_FL_KEEP_SIZE only no change

docs.title: Block granularity
docs.text: The backend implementation uses 131 072-byte blocks; the running FUSE path uses 65 536-byte blocks (see Dual-Interface Architecture).

docs.title: Specification requirements
docs.text:
KernelOffloadingAcceleration is built from these requirement classes. Each is declared in spec/ and listed in the feature's deps.

CopyFileRangeReq

spec.offload.CopyFileRangeReq

Intercepts the FUSE copy_file_range callback triggered by cp, sendfile, or copy_file_range(2) syscalls, executing server-side block duplication directly inside PostgreSQL.

Technical Details:

  • Intercepts copy_file_range(ino_in, off_in, ino_out, off_out, len, flags).
  • Executes INSERT INTO blocks SELECT ... or CoW block ref-linking inside PostgreSQL without streaming payload bytes through FUSE daemon memory buffers.
  • Updates target entry size, mtime, and ctime metadata atomically in a single transaction.
FallocatePunchHoleReq

spec.offload.FallocatePunchHoleReq

Intercepts the FUSE fallocate callback for block allocation and sparse hole punching (FALLOC_FL_PUNCH_HOLE).

Technical Details:

  • For FALLOC_FL_PUNCH_HOLE | FALLOC_FL_KEEP_SIZE, deletes block records in the target byte range DELETE FROM blocks WHERE ino = $1 AND block_no >= $2 AND block_no <= $3.
  • For standard pre-allocation (FALLOC_FL_KEEP_SIZE), creates zero-filled block placeholders or updates entry size metadata without physical byte copying.
ReflinkBlockSharingReq

spec.offload.ReflinkBlockSharingReq

Implements reference-counted Copy-on-Write (CoW) block storage for instant file cloning (cp --reflink=always).

Technical Details:

  • Introduces a block_id and ref_count column or block reference mapping table.
  • Offloaded file copies simply copy block references and increment ref_count in $O(1)$ time.
  • Write operations on shared blocks perform lazy Copy-on-Write allocation (write_block), allocating a private block copy only when modified.
CloneSubtreeReq

spec.offload.CloneSubtreeReq

Enables server-side recursive directory tree cloning via custom ioctl or extended attribute (xattr) calls.

Technical Details:

  • Intercepts subtree clone requests for a target directory inode.
  • Executes recursive set-based INSERT INTO entries SELECT ... and INSERT INTO blocks SELECT ... queries inside a single PostgreSQL transaction.
  • Clones complex multi-gigabyte directory hierarchies in milliseconds.
ContentSearchOffloadReq

spec.offload.ContentSearchOffloadReq

Offloads file content searching (grep, find) to PostgreSQL GIN and pg_trgm trigram indices.

Technical Details:

  • Maintains GIN/trigram indices over blocks.data or extracted text.
  • Exposes custom search queries (via xattr or virtual /proc/control paths) returning matching inode lists or line offsets directly from database index scans, bypassing full file reads over FUSE.

docs.title: Reference: Observability & Diagnostics
docs.text:
Status: Stable

Tracing, the 60-second metrics, the SIGUSR1 state dump, error chains and crash reports all ship today. Of the per-errno counters, only eio and enoent are incremented yet.

Operators can see what the daemon is doing, how fast it is doing it, and why something failed, from the log alone: structured spans for every operation, periodic metrics, an on-demand state dump, and self-contained error chains and crash reports.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.text: Setting Values Default RUST_LOG tracing-subscriber EnvFilter syntax pgfs=info RUST_LOG_FORMAT json for newline-delimited JSON; anything else for text text Destination stderr

docs.text:

Expected conditions (ENOENT, EEXIST, ENOTEMPTY, EISDIR, ENOTDIR, EINVAL) are replied without logging.

docs.text:
Histogram Records fuse wall-clock time of every instrumented FUSE callback db wall-clock time of every Db method

Buckets: <=10, <=100, <=1k, <=10k, <=100k, <=1M, >1M microseconds. Each percentile is reported as the upper bound of the bucket that contains it.

docs.title: Error chain format
docs.text:
Unexpected failures are logged at ERROR as one line, the anyhow alternate ({:#}) rendering of the chain, inside the span of the FUSE callback that failed:

ERROR <callback>{<span fields>}: pgfs::fs: <what was attempted> (at src/<file>.rs:<line>): <deeper context> (at …): <root cause>

Example:

ERROR lookup{parent=1 name=after-stop}: pgfs::fs: get attributes of entry "after-stop" in "" (at src/db.rs:453): db error: FATAL: terminating connection due to administrator command

Startup failures are printed to stderr in the same form, prefixed pgfs:, and the process exits with status 1.

docs.text:
Written to stderr and logged at ERROR before the process unwinds or aborts:

panic at <file>:<line>: <message>
pgfs v<version> on <os>/<arch>, built with <rustc version>, RUST_BACKTRACE=<value>
Backtrace:
<backtrace>

docs.text: Thread Role signal-waiter receives SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP, SIGUSR1, SIGUSR2 metrics-export logs metrics every 60 s liveness heartbeat every 10 s deadlock-watchdog unmounts when a stall is detected

docs.title: Specification requirements
docs.text:
ObservableDaemon is built from these requirement classes. Each is declared in spec/ and listed in the feature's deps.

UsesStructuredTracing

spec.app.UsesStructuredTracing

The daemon uses the tracing crate (not bare log/env_logger) for all diagnostic output. The tracing-subscriber subscriber is initialized before any other work. RUST_LOG controls filter levels with the same syntax as env_logger; RUST_LOG_FORMAT=json switches to machine-parseable JSON output.

InstrumentsFuseCallbacks

spec.app.InstrumentsFuseCallbacks

Every Filesystem callback (lookup, getattr, read, write, create, mkdir, unlink, rmdir, rename, readdir, setattr, open, flush, fsync, copy_file_range, fallocate) opens a tracing::info_span! recording ino and name (where applicable). The span is entered for the duration of the callback so nested DB operations are automatically attributed.

InstrumentsDbOperations

spec.app.InstrumentsDbOperations

Every Db method (getattr, read, write, create, mkdir, unlink, rmdir, rename, list) opens a tracing::debug_span! recording the (parent, name) key. The span is entered for the duration of the database round-trip.

DistinguishesExpectedErrors

spec.app.DistinguishesExpectedErrors

Expected conditions (ENOENT, EEXIST, ENOTEMPTY, EISDIR, ENOTDIR, EINVAL) are replied directly to the kernel without logging. Unexpected failures (database errors, invariant violations) are logged in full via log_and_reply! with the complete error chain and replied as EIO.

ExportsPeriodicMetrics

spec.app.ExportsPeriodicMetrics

A background thread logs five INFO lines every 60 s: metrics|ops|… (per-callback counters), metrics|errors|… (EIO and per-errno counters), metrics|replica|reads=… fallbacks=…, metrics|latency|fuse=… and metrics|latency|db=…. Counters are lifetime totals and never reset. Latency histograms bucket wall-clock durations at ≤10µs, ≤100µs, ≤1ms, ≤10ms, ≤100ms, ≤1s and >1s and report p50/p95/p99 as the upper bound of the bucket that contains the percentile.

DumpsStateOnSigusr1

spec.app.DumpsStateOnSigusr1

SIGUSR1 sets a flag on the signal-waiter thread. The next FUSE callback clears it and logs, at INFO, state|ino_cache=… next_ino=… db=connected (replica none|fresh|stale or unreachable) uptime_secs=… followed by the FUSE and DB latency summaries. The dump never runs on the signal thread and never blocks dispatch; on an idle mount it appears with the next filesystem access.

WritesHealthFiles

spec.app.WritesHealthFiles

After connecting to Postgres the daemon writes its PID to /tmp/pgfs-<hash>.pid, prints health pid file: <path> on stdout and logs it. After the FUSE session is created it writes /tmp/pgfs-<hash>.ready containing ready. <hash> is 16 hex digits derived from the mountpoint argument exactly as given. Both files are removed when run() returns.

ReportsCrashes

spec.app.ReportsCrashes

If the daemon panics, the panic hook emits a crash report to both stderr and the log channel. The report includes the panic message, file:line location, a symbolized backtrace, and OS/Rust metadata. In release builds, panic = "abort" prevents a broken daemon from lingering.

docs.title: Reference: On-Demand Profiling
docs.text:
Status: Stable

The SIGUSR2 CPU profiler, the Chrome span trace and scripts/bench_profile.sh ship today behind the profiling Cargo feature. Default builds contain none of it.

Operators can profile a running pgfs daemon without restarting it: SIGUSR2 starts and stops a CPU sampler that writes a flamegraph, and a span trace of every FUSE callback and database call is written on shutdown. All of it is compiled in only with the profiling feature.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Specification requirements
docs.text:
OnDemandProfiling is built from these requirement classes. Each is declared in spec/ and listed in the feature's deps.

CpuProfilingOnDemand

spec.perf.CpuProfilingOnDemand

SIGUSR2 toggles a pprof CPU sampler running at 997 Hz. The toggle runs entirely on the signal-waiter thread; signal dispositions never do the work themselves. A second SIGUSR2 stops sampling and renders the report.

Output contract — stopping writes two files under /tmp:

  • /tmp/pgfs-profile-{ts}.svg — flamegraph (inferno SVG)
  • /tmp/pgfs-profile-{ts}.stacks — per-stack sample dump The written path is logged at info!. The .pb protobuf format is deliberately not produced (the protobuf codec feature is not enabled); the SVG and stack dump carry the same information.
SpanTraceOnShutdown

spec.perf.SpanTraceOnShutdown

When built with the profiling feature, a tracing-chrome layer is installed in the tracing subscriber at startup. It captures every FUSE callback span and nested db:: span. On clean shutdown the trace is written to /tmp/pgfs-trace-{ts}.json (Chrome/Perfetto format). The target path is logged at info! at startup.

ZeroOverheadWhenDisabled

spec.perf.ZeroOverheadWhenDisabled

All profiling code — the pprof guard, the chrome layer, and report rendering — is gated behind the profiling feature. A default build contains no profiling instructions; SIGUSR2 merely logs that profiling was not compiled in. cargo check, cargo clippy, and cargo test must all pass with and without the feature.

ProfileDrivenBenchmark

spec.perf.ProfileDrivenBenchmark

scripts/bench_profile.sh drives the mounted filesystem through workload phases — sequential small-block writes (whole-blob read-modify-write amplification), sequential reads, and many-small-file creation (round-trip bound) — each wrapped in a SIGUSR2 start/stop pair. The bottleneck shows up as CPU time in the flamegraph rather than as wall-clock guesswork, and the span trace attributes FUSE vs DB time.

docs.title: Reference: Performance Optimizations
docs.text:
Status: Partially implemented

Chunked blocks, prepared statements, asynchronous commit, unlogged tables, per-handle write buffering, transaction batching and the attribute-cache TTL are implemented. Inode-keyed storage, the multi-threaded connection pool and the kernel writeback cache are not. The Reference page has the per-requirement status.

pgfs incorporates a structured performance optimization pipeline targeting database access latency, connection concurrency, userspace buffering, and FUSE kernel-transport tuning.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Command-line options
docs.text: Option Default Effect --attr-ttl <seconds> 1.0 TTL attached to every attribute and entry reply; fractional values allowed --unlogged off create entries and blocks as UNLOGGED tables; no effect on existing tables

docs.text:
Setting Value Block size (FUSE path) 65 536 bytes synchronous_commit off, set on every pooled connection Connection pool r2d2, max 10 per pool; the daemon holds 1 primary connection (plus 1 standby connection) for its lifetime FUSE dispatch single-threaded Kernel capabilities requested FUSE_BIG_WRITES Replica freshness cache 500 ms Prepared on connect getattr, create, mkdir, unlink, rmdir, list, read_blocks, upsert_block, prune_blocks, delete_blocks, and six inode-keyed statements

Replica queries, rename, size updates and rmdir's emptiness check use unprepared SQL.

docs.title: Requirement status
docs.text: Requirement Status Notes ChunkedBlockStorageReq implemented 64 KiB blocks in blocks(parent, name, block_no) InoBasedRekeyingReq partial ino/parent_ino columns and prepared statements exist; the FUSE path is still keyed by path and leaves them at their defaults SparseWritePaddingReq partial unbuffered writes merge with the stored block; writes buffered on an open handle do not, see BufferedWriteFlushReq ReplicaFreshnessCacheReq implemented 500 ms monotonic TTL PreparedStatementReq implemented hot-path primary statements; see list above SynchronousCommitTuningReq implemented always on; not configurable UnloggedTableOptReq implemented --unlogged TransactionBatchingReq implemented write_range, truncate, the buffered flush and rename are single transactions; unlink and rmdir are separate statements MultiThreadedConnectionPoolReq partial the pool exists but one connection is used and dispatch is single-threaded; no --max-pool-size BufferedWriteFlushReq implemented per open handle; flushed on flush, fsync, release and before a read of the same file; buffered blocks start empty rather than from the stored block KernelAttrCacheTtlReq implemented --attr-ttl KernelWritebackCacheReq not implemented only FUSE_BIG_WRITES is negotiated; no --writeback-cache

docs.title: Specification requirements
docs.text:
OptimizationRoadmap is built from these requirement classes. Each is declared in spec/ and listed in the feature's deps.

ChunkedBlockStorageReq

spec.optimize.ChunkedBlockStorageReq

File contents are stored in fixed-size block chunks (64KB or 128KB) in a blocks(ino, block_no, data) table rather than monolithic byte blobs in entries.data.

Technical Details:

  • Read operations calculate block ranges [start_block..end_block] based on offset and size, fetching only touched blocks from PostgreSQL.
  • Write operations update or upsert only touched block records rather than rewriting the entire file payload.
  • Truncation via setattr deletes block records where block_no > new_size / block_size and trims trailing block bytes.
  • Metadata (size, mtime, ctime) remains in entries as the source of truth.
InoBasedRekeyingReq

spec.optimize.InoBasedRekeyingReq

Rekey entries and blocks tables from (parent, name) text keys to 64-bit integer ino BIGSERIAL primary keys (entries(ino) and blocks(ino, block_no)).

Technical Details:

  • entries table uses ino BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY and parent_ino BIGINT REFERENCES entries(ino).
  • Directory rename(old_parent, old_name, new_parent, new_name) updates parent_ino = new_parent and name = new_name on a single row in $O(1)$ time, eliminating $O(N)$ cascading string updates.
  • Path lookup is accelerated via B-Tree index on (parent_ino, name).
  • Inode numbers are guaranteed stable for open file handles and kernel VFS stat callbacks.
SparseWritePaddingReq

spec.optimize.SparseWritePaddingReq

Unaligned or sparse block writes (where offset_in_block > 0 on an uninstantiated block record) zero-pad preceding bytes at the application layer before upserting to prevent byte-0 data corruption.

Technical Details:

  • When write_block(ino, block_no, data, offset_in_block) is called for a block that does not yet exist in blocks, the engine checks if offset_in_block > 0.
  • If offset_in_block > 0, the engine constructs a zero-filled byte array of length offset_in_block and prepends it to data before upserting.
  • Subsequent reads of [0..offset_in_block] correctly return zero-filled bytes conforming to POSIX sparse file behavior.
ReplicaFreshnessCacheReq

spec.optimize.ReplicaFreshnessCacheReq

When running with --replica, the replica freshness check (replica_fresh) caches its health and WAL LSN verdict using an atomic TTL cache to eliminate per-read validation overhead.

Technical Details:

  • Uses AtomicBool for freshness state and AtomicU64 for timestamp tracking.
  • Re-evaluates Postgres physical streaming standby lag (pg_is_in_recovery, pg_current_wal_lsn, pg_last_wal_replay_lsn) only when now - last_checked > 500ms.
  • Consecutive read operations reuse the cached verdict, reducing query overhead by 75% while ensuring automatic fallback to primary if lag exceeds tolerance.
PreparedStatementReq

spec.optimize.PreparedStatementReq

All static SQL queries (getattr, read, write, create, mkdir, unlink, rmdir, list, rename) are pre-compiled as prepared statements upon database connection initialization.

Technical Details:

  • Pre-compiles statement handles (stmt_getattr, stmt_read_blocks, stmt_upsert_block, etc.) during DbPool::get() or worker initialization.
  • Eliminates SQL lexical parsing, semantic analysis, and query planning overhead from the FUSE operation hot path.
SynchronousCommitTuningReq

spec.optimize.SynchronousCommitTuningReq

The database layer supports connection-level tuning of synchronous_commit (SET synchronous_commit = off) to optimize per-operation fsync latency.

Technical Details:

  • Executed during connection acquisition (on_acquire hook in connection pool manager).
  • Allows transactions to return immediately after writing to Postgres WAL buffers, trading a sub-second crash durability window for up to 10x higher metadata IOPS.
UnloggedTableOptReq

spec.optimize.UnloggedTableOptReq

The database schema supports creating entries and blocks as UNLOGGED tables for high-performance development, caching, and testing workloads.

Technical Details:

  • DDL specifies CREATE UNLOGGED TABLE entries and CREATE UNLOGGED TABLE blocks.
  • Bypasses WAL logging entirely, maximizing raw write throughput for ephemeral mounts.
TransactionBatchingReq

spec.optimize.TransactionBatchingReq

FUSE operations that execute multiple sequential database queries wrap them in a single explicit database transaction.

Technical Details:

  • Groups multi-query operations (e.g. truncate + write, directory deletion checks) within BEGIN ... COMMIT blocks.
  • Reduces network round-trips and WAL commit fsync overhead from $N$ commits to 1 commit.
MultiThreadedConnectionPoolReq

spec.optimize.MultiThreadedConnectionPoolReq

The database client uses a thread-safe connection pool (r2d2 or bb8), combined with multi-worker FUSE session dispatch to process parallel operations concurrently.

Technical Details:

  • Configures pool size via CLI --max-pool-size.
  • Replaces single-threaded &mut self Db handles with pooled connection acquisition per thread.
BufferedWriteFlushReq

spec.optimize.BufferedWriteFlushReq

Small or non-aligned FUSE write calls buffer dirty byte ranges or blocks in memory per open file handle, flushing pending writes to PostgreSQL on flush, release, or explicit fsync.

Technical Details:

  • Maintains a per-fd dirty block buffer in daemon memory.
  • Aggregates page-sized kernel writes into full 128KB block writes before issuing database upserts.
KernelAttrCacheTtlReq

spec.optimize.KernelAttrCacheTtlReq

The kernel attribute and entry cache TTL is configurable via a CLI option (--attr-ttl), reducing repetitive lookup and getattr FUSE callbacks.

Technical Details:

  • Sets TTL duration in fuser::ReplyAttr and fuser::ReplyEntry responses.
  • Bypasses daemon and database queries for stat/lookup ops on unchanged paths during TTL window.
KernelWritebackCacheReq

spec.optimize.KernelWritebackCacheReq

FUSE callback initialization negotiates kernel capabilities including FUSE_WRITEBACK_CACHE and splice read/write.

Technical Details:

  • Enables CAP_WRITEBACK_CACHE in KernelConfig during FUSE init.
  • Allows Linux VFS page cache to coalesce small sequential write syscalls into 128KB block buffers.

docs.title: Reference: Reliable Mount & Shutdown
docs.text:
Status: Stable

AutoUnmount, signal-driven clean unmount, the deadlock watchdog, health files and the pgfs.sh escalation path are all implemented.

The filesystem mounts and unmounts cleanly. Crashing or killing the daemon never leaves a ghost mount behind.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.text: Option Value fsname pgfs auto_unmount requested; if the mount fails with it, pgfs logs a WARN and retries without it Kernel capability negotiated in init FUSE_BIG_WRITES

docs.title: Startup sequence
docs.text:
1. Initialise logging; install the panic hook.
  2. Block SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP, SIGUSR1 and SIGUSR2 in every thread, so a signal that arrives during startup waits instead of killing the process.
  3. Connect to PostgreSQL and create the schema if needed.
  4. Write /tmp/pgfs-<hash>.pid; print and log its path.
  5. Create the FUSE session (mount).
  6. Write /tmp/pgfs-<hash>.ready.
  7. Start the liveness, metrics, deadlock-watchdog and signal-waiter threads.
  8. Serve FUSE requests until unmounted.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
Signal Effect SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP clean unmount; the daemon exits with status 0 SIGUSR1 state dump on the next FUSE callback (see Observability) SIGUSR2 toggle CPU profiling (see On-Demand Profiling) SIGKILL, crash, OOM kill the kernel removes the mount (AutoUnmount); health files remain

Signals are received with sigwait on a dedicated signal-waiter thread, never in an asynchronous handler.

docs.title: Health files
docs.text:
File Written Contents Removed /tmp/pgfs-<hash>.pid after the database connection succeeds daemon PID on clean exit /tmp/pgfs-<hash>.ready after the mount is created ready on clean exit

<hash> is 16 hex digits computed from the mountpoint argument exactly as given, so ./mnt and /abs/path/mnt produce different names.

docs.title: Deadlock watchdog
docs.text: Parameter Value Heartbeat period 10 s Stall threshold 30 s without a heartbeat, observed by a FUSE callback Action ERROR log; the callback replies EIO; the watchdog unmounts Unmount retries 5, 500 ms apart; then the process exits with status 1

docs.title: Database connection lifetime
docs.text: The daemon acquires one primary connection (and one standby connection with --replica) at startup and keeps it until exit. It does not reconnect. If PostgreSQL restarts or the connection drops, every operation that reaches the database replies EIO until the daemon is restarted. The mount itself stays up and still unmounts cleanly.

docs.title: Panics
docs.text: Build Behaviour debug the panic hook writes the crash report, then the panic unwinds release the panic hook writes the crash report, then the process aborts (panic = "abort") and the kernel removes the mount

docs.title: Exit status
docs.text: Status Cause 0 clean unmount 1 startup failure (error chain printed as pgfs: …), or the deadlock watchdog gave up

docs.title: Specification requirements
docs.text:
ReliableMount is built from these requirement classes. Each is declared in spec/ and listed in the feature's deps.

MountsCleanly

spec.app.MountsCleanly

The daemon mounts a FUSE filesystem at the given mountpoint using AutoUnmount so the kernel removes the mount if the process exits for any reason. The mountpoint must be an existing, empty directory not already mounted.

HandlesShutdownSignals

spec.app.HandlesShutdownSignals

SIGINT, SIGTERM, and SIGHUP trigger a clean unmount via session.unmount(). If the clean unmount fails, AutoUnmount guarantees the kernel still removes the mount. Signal handling uses a dedicated sigwait thread so it never blocks FUSE dispatch.

DetectsDeadlock

spec.app.DetectsDeadlock

A liveness thread increments a counter every 10 s. Every FUSE callback checks it on entry; if the counter has not advanced for 30 s the callback logs ERROR, replies EIO and flags a watchdog thread. The watchdog unmounts cleanly, retrying up to 5 times 500 ms apart, and exits the process if every attempt fails so that AutoUnmount removes the mount. The check uses a monotonic clock, so wall-clock jumps never cause false positives.

WritesHealthFiles

spec.app.WritesHealthFiles

After connecting to Postgres the daemon writes its PID to /tmp/pgfs-<hash>.pid, prints health pid file: <path> on stdout and logs it. After the FUSE session is created it writes /tmp/pgfs-<hash>.ready containing ready. <hash> is 16 hex digits derived from the mountpoint argument exactly as given. Both files are removed when run() returns.

ProvidesLifecycleScript

spec.app.ProvidesLifecycleScript

scripts/pgfs.sh up|down|status|run owns the mount lifecycle. up starts Postgres if needed, runs cargo build, sweeps a stale mount whose daemon is gone, starts target/debug/pgfs detached with output appended to testdata/pgfs.log, and waits up to 10 s for the mount to appear in /proc/mounts. down sends SIGTERM, waits up to 10 s, then escalates to fusermount3 -u, reports the holders of a busy mount, and finally lazy-unmounts. status reports mount, daemon and Postgres state and flags ghost mounts. run builds and execs the daemon in the foreground. docs.title: Reference: Replicated Storage
docs.text:
Status: Partially implemented

Write routing, lag detection, transparent fallback and the Docker standby work today. File contents (read) are still always served by the primary, and a standby that is unreachable when the daemon starts is dropped for the daemon's lifetime without a warning.

A pgfs mount can be backed by a primary Postgres and a physical streaming standby in Docker. Writes go to the primary; reads are served from whichever node is authoritative at that instant, falling back to the primary when the standby lags. The filesystem is eventually consistent with the standby's lag continuously bounded by the freshness check, and a standby failure never causes data loss or a kernel-visible error.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

docs.title: Command line
docs.text: Option Meaning --replica <libpq string> connection to a physical streaming standby; optional

docs.title: Operation routing
docs.text: Operation Served by lookup, getattr standby when fresh, otherwise primary readdir standby when fresh, otherwise primary read (file contents) primary, always create, mkdir, write, flush, fsync, setattr, unlink, rmdir, rename primary checks that decide a mutation (existence for create/mkdir/rmdir, source and target for rename, setattr) primary

docs.title: Freshness
docs.text:
A standby is fresh when either query below holds; any error on either node means not fresh.

Condition Query standby is not in recovery (it is itself a primary) SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() on the standby returns false standby has replayed everything the primary has written pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() on the standby ≥ pg_current_wal_lsn() on the primary Property Value Verdict cache 500 ms (FRESHNESS_TTL_MS) Clock monotonic Staleness bound a cached "fresh" verdict is reused for up to 500 ms, so a read can reach the standby up to 500 ms after the primary moved ahead of it, including right after this daemon's own write

docs.text:
Event Effect standby stale or unreachable at read time the read is served by the primary; no error reaches the kernel first fallback in each 60 s metrics period WARN reads falling back to primary (standby stale or unreachable) later fallbacks DEBUG read served from primary (replica stale) every fallback metrics|replica fallbacks incremented

File-content reads always use the primary and count as fallbacks.

docs.title: Specification requirements
docs.text:
ReplicatedFilesystem is built from these requirement classes. Each is declared in spec/ and listed in the feature's deps.

StartsDockerStandby

spec.replica.StartsDockerStandby

scripts/replica_db.sh provisions a Docker container running a physical streaming standby of the pgfs primary. The standby image is postgres:17, matching the primary's major version (pg_basebackup refuses cross-version replication). The standby data directory is produced by pg_basebackup over TCP loopback (127.0.0.1:5432) with -R so standby.signal and primary_conninfo are written, then the container runs postgres in recovery, streaming WAL continuously.

The container publishes the standby on 127.0.0.1:5433 (host loopback only, never 0.0.0.0). The script is idempotent: up re-provisions only if the standby data is absent, down stops the container but keeps the data volume, wipe removes both. Every step surfaces a full error chain on failure (see err.Err).

RequiresPrimaryTcpListener

spec.replica.RequiresPrimaryTcpListener

Physical replication requires the primary to accept TCP on loopback: init_db.sh starts postgres with -h 127.0.0.1 (in addition to the project-local Unix socket) so pg_basebackup and the WAL sender can reach it. The primary never listens on a non-loopback interface; pg_hba.conf already contains host replication all 127.0.0.1/32 trust. The daemon does not change this behavior when --replica is absent.

AcceptsReplicaConnection

spec.replica.AcceptsReplicaConnection

The daemon accepts an optional --replica <libpq-conn> argument on top of --conn. When provided, it opens a second postgres::Client to the standby; the standby is never schema-initialized (it is a physical copy). When absent, the daemon behaves exactly as today: one connection, all operations on the primary.

ServesReadsFromReplica

spec.replica.ServesReadsFromReplica

Read-only operations — getattr, list (readdir), and read — are served from the replica client when it is fresh. Each read re-evaluates freshness so the source adapts to replication state. Read routing is recorded in the metrics (REPLICA_READ_COUNT) and a DEBUG log line names the source used.

WritesStayOnPrimary

spec.replica.WritesStayOnPrimary

Every mutating operation — create, mkdir, write, unlink, rmdir, and rename — executes on the primary client, never the replica. Internal consistency reads that a mutation depends on (e.g. rename's source-existence check) also read the primary directly so a stale replica can never corrupt a transaction's decision.

DetectsReplicationLag

spec.replica.DetectsReplicationLag

A replica is fresh iff the standby is in recovery and its replay position (pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() - '0/0'::pg_lsn) is at or ahead of the primary's current position (pg_current_wal_lsn() - '0/0'). If the standby is not in recovery (it is itself a primary), it is treated as fresh. Any error querying either node means not fresh. The freshness query is cheap (two scalar reads) and runs per read.

ReplicaFreshnessCacheReq

spec.optimize.ReplicaFreshnessCacheReq

When running with --replica, the replica freshness check (replica_fresh) caches its health and WAL LSN verdict using an atomic TTL cache to eliminate per-read validation overhead.

Technical Details:

  • Uses AtomicBool for freshness state and AtomicU64 for timestamp tracking.
  • Re-evaluates Postgres physical streaming standby lag (pg_is_in_recovery, pg_current_wal_lsn, pg_last_wal_replay_lsn) only when now - last_checked > 500ms.
  • Consecutive read operations reuse the cached verdict, reducing query overhead by 75% while ensuring automatic fallback to primary if lag exceeds tolerance.
FallsBackToPrimary

spec.replica.FallsBackToPrimary

When the replica is absent, unreachable, or not fresh, reads are served from the primary with no error surfaced to the kernel — a replicated mount degrades to a single-node mount. The first fallback per period is logged at WARN; every fallback increments REPLICA_FALLBACK_COUNT. A stale replica never produces stale reads, only primary reads.

ReplicaObservability

spec.replica.ReplicaObservability

Replication state is observable: the 60-second metrics export includes metrics|replica|reads=.. fallbacks=.., the startup log announces replica mode and the replica connection string, and the SIGUSR1 state dump reports replica freshness. Daemon startup succeeds even when --replica points at an unreachable standby — it is logged at WARN and the mount runs primary-only.

docs.title: Reference: Sharded Filesystem
docs.text:
Status: Planned, not implemented

Specified and designed (design/sharded_filesystem.md), not implemented. The daemon does not accept --shards or --replication-factor, and scripts/shard_db.sh does not exist yet. The tutorial and how-to describe the intended interface.

A pgfs mount can be backed by N independent Postgres host nodes with RAID-5-like subset replication: each directory subtree is pinned to a replication set of R of the N hosts (never a full mirror on every host). Writes fan out to every member of the set; reads consult a quorum and return the newest version. Any number of clients can mount the same namespace from different machines and add files to one shared tree, and a host failure degrades reads and writes to the remaining healthy members without stale or corrupt data.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

All items on this page are planned. Values come from design/sharded_filesystem.md (Draft 0.1.0).

docs.text: Option Meaning --shards <CONN[,CONN,…]> the N host connection strings; enables sharded mode; mutually exclusive with --replica --replication-factor <R> members per replication set; default 3; must be ≤ N --attr-ttl <secs> bounds cross-client staleness; default 1.0

docs.text: Term Definition host one PostgreSQL instance, identified by a connection string replication set an ordered list of R hosts that hold the same entries set_id small stable integer naming a replication set quorum ⌊R/2⌋ + 1 members of a set subtree everything under one top-level name set leader the set member that allocates inode numbers

docs.text: Rule Detail Key the entry's top-level ancestor name Function consistent hashing over the ring of replication sets Stickiness every descendant of a top-level name lives on the same set Root (inode 1) replicated on every host

docs.text: Property Value Encoding (set_id << 48) | local_seq Allocator the set leader's entries_ino_seq, seeded at set_id << 48 Leader failure the next healthy member allocates from a disjoint reserved range Cross-set rename keeps the inode number

docs.title: Specification requirements
docs.text:
ShardedFilesystem is built from these requirement classes. Each is declared in spec/ and listed in the feature's deps.

AcceptsShardTopology

spec.shard.AcceptsShardTopology

The daemon accepts --shards <CONN[,CONN,…]> listing the N host connection strings and --replication-factor <R> (default 3, must be ≤ N). When --shards is present, the daemon runs in sharded mode and builds the consistent-hash ring from the host list; the existing --conn / --replica single-node and physical-standby modes are unchanged when --shards is absent.

ComputesDeterministicPlacement

spec.shard.ComputesDeterministicPlacement

Every client computes the same replication set for a given entry from its top-level ancestor name using consistent hashing over the ring of N hosts with factor R — no shared placement table is needed. Placement is subtree-sticky: all descendants of a top-level directory live on the same replication set, so readdir is a single-set query rather than a cluster-wide merge.

ReplicatesToSubsetOfHosts

spec.shard.ReplicatesToSubsetOfHosts

Each entry is replicated to exactly R of the N hosts (a replication set) — the RAID-5-like partial mirror. The root directory (ino=1) is the only exception and is replicated on every host so any client can list /. Data is never copied to all N hosts.

AllocatesGloballyUniqueInodes

spec.shard.AllocatesGloballyUniqueInodes

Inodes are unique across the whole namespace even though each host runs an independent Postgres instance with its own identity sequence. The global inode encodes the entry's replication set id in the high bits: ino = (set_id << 48) | local_seq. The root keeps ino=1. A cross-set rename retains the inode, so uniqueness is preserved.

AllocatesInodesViaSetLeader

spec.shard.AllocatesInodesViaSetLeader

Each replication set designates one healthy member (the set leader, chosen deterministically in ring order) as the inode authority. The leader's entries_ino_seq is seeded to start at (set_id << 48), so INSERT … RETURNING ino yields globally unique values. The client allocates against the leader, then fans the explicit ino out to the other R−1 members. If the leader is unreachable, the next healthy member takes over from a disjoint reserved region so allocations never overlap the departed leader's range.

ServesReadsFromReplicationSet

spec.shard.ServesReadsFromReplicationSet

Read-only operations — getattr, lookup, readdir, and read — are resolved to the entry's replication set and served from its members. A versioned quorum read picks the row with the highest ver; ties are broken deterministically. Reads skip hosts currently marked degraded.

VersionsMutations

spec.shard.VersionsMutations

Every mutation stamps the entry with a monotonically increasing logical version ver = (client_id << 32) | client_local_seq. ver is globally comparable without wall-clock coordination between hosts, so concurrent writers to the same entry resolve to last-writer-wins by version.

FansOutWritesToSetMembers

spec.shard.FansOutWritesToSetMembers

Every mutation — create, mkdir, write, unlink, rmdir, rename — executes as a single transaction on every member of the entry's replication set (fan-out), with followers inserting the explicit ino/ver supplied by the client. Consistency reads that a mutation depends on (rename's source-existence check, rmdir's emptiness check) read from the same set with the same quorum rule, never from a possibly-stale degraded member.

RequiresWriteQuorum

spec.shard.RequiresWriteQuorum

A mutation succeeds only when at least QUORUM = ⌊R/2⌋ + 1 members acknowledge it; unacknowledged members are marked degraded. If fewer than quorum acknowledge, the acknowledged members are rolled back with a compensating delete and the operation replies EIO — a write either lands on a quorum or is not reported as committed.

DegradesGracefullyOnHostFailure

spec.shard.DegradesGracefullyOnHostFailure

A host is marked degraded after K consecutive failures. While degraded, reads skip it and writes fan out only to healthy members, both still requiring quorum. Reads never return stale or corrupt data from a degraded host, and the degraded set is reported in metrics and the SIGUSR1 state dump. A recovering host is verified against the highest ver per entry and missing mutations are re-applied.

SupportsCrossSetRename

spec.shard.SupportsCrossSetRename

rename whose source and destination live in different replication sets snapshots the source subtree from a healthy member, applies it to the destination set (new parent/name, retained ino, bumped ver), then deletes the source rows — all quorum-acked, with compensating rollback on the destination if either half fails. Re-lands atomically or is unchanged. Ordinary renames inside one subtree stay single-set local updates.

SupportsSharedMounts

spec.shard.SupportsSharedMounts

Multiple pgfs daemons on different machines can mount the same namespace by passing the same --shards topology. Identical placement computation and collision-free inode allocation let any client read and add files to one shared tree. Cross-client visibility is bounded by attr_ttl with write-through caching; strongly consistent kernel cache coherence via leases is future work.

ShardObservability

spec.shard.ShardObservability

Sharded-mode operation is observable: the 60-second metrics export includes SHARD_READ_COUNT, SHARD_WRITE_COUNT, SHARD_QUORUM_MISSES, SHARD_FALLBACK_COUNT, and SHARD_DEGRADED_HOSTS; the startup log announces the topology (N hosts, R, ring seed); and the SIGUSR1 state dump reports the ring, per-set membership, per-host health, degraded set, and leader state.

docs.title: Tutorial: Atomic Rename
docs.text:
Status: Stable

File and directory renames, overwrite semantics and the full POSIX error matrix are implemented and covered by test_rename.sh and test_git_init.sh. renameat2 flags (RENAME_NOREPLACE, RENAME_EXCHANGE) are rejected.

Users can rename (move) files and directories with standard mv semantics, including overwriting existing files and empty directories.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

In this tutorial we will rename files and whole directory trees, overwrite a file atomically, see which renames pgfs refuses, and finish by running git (which depends on atomic rename) inside the mount.

We need a running mount; see Your first pgfs mount.

docs.title: Step 1: rename over an existing file
docs.text:
mkdir testdata/mnt/rename && cd testdata/mnt/rename
echo v1 > a.txt
echo v2 > b.txt
mv a.txt b.txt
cat b.txt
ls

v1
b.txt

b.txt now holds what a.txt held, and a.txt is gone.

docs.title: Step 2: move a directory with everything in it
docs.text:
mkdir -p old/inner
echo deep > old/inner/file.txt
mv old new
cat new/inner/file.txt

deep

docs.title: Step 3: see what pgfs refuses
docs.text:
A directory cannot move inside itself:

mv new new/inner/x

mv: cannot move 'new' to a subdirectory of itself, 'new/inner/x'

A directory cannot replace a non-empty directory:

mkdir -p full && touch full/f
mkdir empty
mv -T empty full

mv: cannot overwrite 'full': Directory not empty

docs.title: Step 4: run git
docs.text:
Git takes a lock by creating config.lock, writes the new configuration into it, and renames it over config. Each commit does the same with branch references.

git init -q repo && cd repo
echo hello > README
git add README
git -c user.name=Tutorial -c user.email=tutorial@example.com commit -qm "first commit"
git log --oneline

511658a first commit

Your commit hash will differ.

docs.title: Step 5: clean up
docs.text:
cd ../../../..
rm -rf testdata/mnt/rename

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
We replaced a file by renaming over it, moved a populated directory in one step, saw the two renames POSIX forbids, and ran a git workflow that depends on all of it. The explanation describes how one database transaction makes this atomic.

docs.title: Tutorial: Dual-Interface Architecture
docs.text:
Status: Planned, not implemented

The PgfsBackend trait, its error mapping and an inode-keyed implementation on Db exist and are unit-tested, but the FUSE layer does not route through them yet. RemoteBackend is a stub, the pgrx engine and the io_uring transport are at the design stage, and there is no --backend option.

pgfs features a Dual-Interface Storage Architecture providing a sub-100µs Local In-Process Engine (pgrx + zero SQL parsing + io_uring zero copy) and a scalable Remote Async Network Engine (tokio-postgres + pipelining).

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

The dual-interface architecture is not wired into the daemon yet, so this tutorial explores the part that exists: the storage seam that both future engines will plug into. We will run its tests, read the trait, and see where the FUSE layer will connect to it. All we need is the repository and the project-local cluster.

docs.title: Step 1: run the backend tests
docs.text:
./scripts/ensure_db.sh
cargo test backend

test backend::tests::test_storage_error_to_libc_errno ... ok
test backend::tests::test_remote_backend_unimplemented_stubs ... ok
test backend::tests::test_file_kind_conversion ... ok
test backend::tests::test_prepare_sparse_block_write_overwrite_existing ... ok
test backend::tests::test_prepare_sparse_block_write_zero_padding ... ok
test db::tests_offload::test_backend_offloaded_copy_file_range_and_fallocate ... ok
test result: ok. 6 passed; 0 failed; ...

docs.title: Step 2: read the trait
docs.text:
grep -n 'async fn' src/backend.rs | head -16

Every method takes inode numbers rather than paths. That is the most important difference from the code that runs today, which keys everything by (parent path, name).

docs.title: Step 3: see how errors become errnos
docs.text:
grep -n -A12 'impl From<StorageError> for libc::c_int' src/backend.rs

A backend reports what went wrong (NotFound, NotEmpty, DatabaseError, ...), and one function turns that into the errno the kernel receives.

docs.title: Step 4: find the seam in the FUSE layer
docs.text:
grep -n 'backend' src/fs.rs | head

PgFs already holds a backend field, constructed as a LocalBackend around the same Db, but the callbacks still call self.db directly. Switching each callback from self.db to self.backend is the next step of this feature.

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
We exercised and read the storage abstraction that will let pgfs choose between an in-process engine and a network engine. The explanation describes where it is heading.

docs.title: Tutorial: Regular Files
docs.text:
Status: Stable

Create, read, write, append, truncate and delete are implemented and covered by unit and integration tests. Permissions, ownership and timestamps are reported but not settable (see Reference).

Users can create, read, write, and delete files through standard POSIX file operations on the mounted directory.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

In this tutorial we will create a file, read it, add to it, cut it short, grow it again, and then look at how its bytes are laid out in PostgreSQL. By the end we will have seen every basic file operation pgfs supports.

We need a running mount. If ./scripts/pgfs.sh status does not say mount: active, follow Your first pgfs mount first, up to Step 2.

docs.title: Step 1: make a workspace
docs.text:
mkdir testdata/mnt/files
cd testdata/mnt/files

docs.title: Step 2: create and read a file
docs.text:
echo 'Hello pgfs' > demo.txt
cat demo.txt

Hello pgfs

docs.title: Step 3: append to it
docs.text:
echo 'More content' >> demo.txt
cat demo.txt
wc -c demo.txt

Hello pgfs
More content
24 demo.txt

docs.title: Step 4: cut it short, then grow it
docs.text:
truncate -s 5 demo.txt
cat demo.txt; echo

Hello

Now grow the file to 10 bytes. The new bytes read back as zeros:

truncate -s 10 demo.txt
od -c demo.txt

0000000   H   e   l   l   o  \0  \0  \0  \0  \0
0000012

docs.title: Step 5: write something bigger
docs.text:
head -c 200000 /dev/urandom > big.bin
cp big.bin copy.bin
cmp big.bin copy.bin && echo identical

identical

docs.title: Step 6: look at the bytes in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
From the repository root, in a second terminal:

psql -h "$PWD/testdata" -d pgfs -c \
  "SELECT name, block_no, length(data) FROM blocks WHERE parent = 'files' ORDER BY name, block_no"

   name   | block_no | length
----------+----------+--------
 big.bin  |        0 |  65536
 big.bin  |        1 |  65536
 big.bin  |        2 |  65536
 big.bin  |        3 |   3392
 copy.bin |        0 |  65536
 ...
 demo.txt |        0 |      5

big.bin is four rows: three full 64 KiB blocks and a short last one. demo.txt is a single 5-byte block. Its declared size is 10, and the five missing bytes are the zeros we saw in Step 4.

docs.title: Step 7: clean up
docs.text:
cd ../../..
rm -r testdata/mnt/files

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
We used ordinary shell tools to exercise create, read, write, append, truncate and delete, and saw that a file's contents are stored as fixed-size blocks. To learn why it is built this way, read the explanation. Next, Directory Trees.

docs.title: Tutorial: Directory Trees
docs.text:
Status: Stable

mkdir, rmdir, readdir and nested paths of any depth are implemented and covered by test_dirs.sh. Directory timestamps are not tracked.

Users can create nested directories, list their contents, and remove empty directories through standard POSIX directory operations.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

In this tutorial we will build a small directory tree, walk it with standard tools, see how it is stored, and take it apart again. We will also meet the one rule directories enforce: they must be empty before they can be removed.

We need a running mount; see Your first pgfs mount if ./scripts/pgfs.sh status does not say mount: active.

docs.title: Step 1: build a tree
docs.text:
cd testdata/mnt
mkdir -p project/src/util project/docs
touch project/src/main.rs project/src/util/strings.rs project/docs/README.md

docs.title: Step 2: walk it
docs.text:
find project | sort

project
project/docs
project/docs/README.md
project/src
project/src/main.rs
project/src/util
project/src/util/strings.rs

ls -la project/src

The listing starts with the . and .. entries, followed by main.rs and util.

docs.title: Step 3: see how the tree is stored
docs.text:
From the repository root, in a second terminal:

psql -h "$PWD/testdata" -d pgfs -c \
  "SELECT parent, name, kind FROM entries
   WHERE parent = 'project' OR starts_with(parent, 'project/')
      OR (parent = '' AND name = 'project')
   ORDER BY parent, name"

      parent       |    name    | kind
-------------------+------------+------
                   | project    | dir
 project           | docs       | dir
 project           | src        | dir
 project/docs      | README.md  | file
 project/src       | main.rs    | file
 project/src       | util       | dir
 project/src/util  | strings.rs | file

Every row names the directory it lives in. project itself lives at the top of the mount, where parent is empty.

docs.title: Step 4: try to remove a directory that is not empty
docs.text:
rmdir project/src

rmdir: failed to remove 'project/src': Directory not empty

docs.title: Step 5: take the tree apart
docs.text:
Empty the directory from the bottom up, and rmdir succeeds:

rm project/src/util/strings.rs
rmdir project/src/util
rm project/src/main.rs
rmdir project/src

Remove the rest in one go:

rm -r project
ls

project no longer appears.

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
We created nested directories, listed them, saw that each entry stores the path of its containing directory, and learned that rmdir only removes empty directories. Next, Atomic Rename moves whole trees in one step.

docs.title: Tutorial: Kernel Offloading
docs.text:
Status: Partially implemented

Server-side copy_file_range and fallocate are implemented in the storage backend and unit-tested, but the FUSE layer does not call them yet. On a mount, copies stream through the daemon and fallocate fails with EOPNOTSUPP. Reflink, subtree clone and content search are planned.

pgfs incorporates Database-Native Kernel Offloading capabilities, utilizing copy_file_range, fallocate, reflink CoW, and server-side search to eliminate userspace byte streaming and deliver sub-millisecond execution for large-scale file operations.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

The offloading callbacks are not connected to the mount yet, but the idea behind them can be tried today with plain SQL. In this tutorial we will copy a file without its bytes ever leaving PostgreSQL, then run the unit test that exercises the real implementation. We need a running mount (see Your first pgfs mount).

docs.title: Step 1: create a file through the mount
docs.text:
mkdir testdata/mnt/offload
head -c 300000 /dev/urandom > testdata/mnt/offload/big.bin

docs.title: Step 2: copy it inside the database
docs.text:
One transaction copies the file's metadata row and its five block rows. No data passes through pgfs or through psql:

psql -h "$PWD/testdata" -d pgfs -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 <<'SQL'
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO entries (parent, name, kind, size)
  SELECT parent, 'clone.bin', kind, size FROM entries
  WHERE parent = 'offload' AND name = 'big.bin';
INSERT INTO blocks (parent, name, block_no, data)
  SELECT parent, 'clone.bin', block_no, data FROM blocks
  WHERE parent = 'offload' AND name = 'big.bin';
COMMIT;
SQL

docs.title: Step 3: see the copy appear on the mount
docs.text:
Wait a second for the kernel's attribute cache to expire, then:

ls -l testdata/mnt/offload
cmp testdata/mnt/offload/big.bin testdata/mnt/offload/clone.bin && echo identical

-rw-r--r-- 1 alice alice 300000 Oct 26 17:13 big.bin
-rw-r--r-- 1 alice alice 300000 Oct 26 17:13 clone.bin
identical

This is what copy_file_range offloading does on the inode-keyed schema: one set-based INSERT … SELECT instead of reading and rewriting every byte.

docs.title: Step 4: run the real implementation's test
docs.text:
cargo test tests_offload

test db::tests_offload::test_backend_offloaded_copy_file_range_and_fallocate ... ok

The test copies 128 KiB between two files with copy_file_range, then punches it back out with fallocate.

docs.title: Step 5: clean up
docs.text: rm -r testdata/mnt/offload

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
We copied a file entirely inside PostgreSQL and saw it through the mount, then ran the backend code that will do the same for cp once it is wired to FUSE. The explanation covers the rest of the plan.

docs.title: Tutorial: Observability & Diagnostics
docs.text:
Status: Stable

Tracing, the 60-second metrics, the SIGUSR1 state dump, error chains and crash reports all ship today. Of the per-errno counters, only eio and enoent are incremented yet.

Operators can see what the daemon is doing, how fast it is doing it, and why something failed, from the log alone: structured spans for every operation, periodic metrics, an on-demand state dump, and self-contained error chains and crash reports.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

In this tutorial we will watch pgfs work: follow its log, ask a running daemon for a state dump, read a metrics report, and then break the database on purpose to see what a real failure looks like. We need a terminal for the daemon and a second one for commands.

docs.title: Step 1: run the daemon in the foreground
docs.text:
In the first terminal:

./scripts/pgfs.sh run

The startup lines show the replica mode, the health file and the negotiated FUSE capability:

INFO pgfs: replica mode: off (single primary)
health pid file: /tmp/pgfs-5049eced64c2821d.pid
INFO init: pgfs::fs: FUSE init: negotiated FUSE_BIG_WRITES

docs.title: Step 2: see that normal misses are quiet
docs.text:
In the second terminal:

cat testdata/mnt/does-not-exist

cat reports "No such file or directory", and the daemon's log stays silent. A missing file is an expected answer, not a failure, so pgfs does not log it.

docs.title: Step 3: ask for a state dump
docs.text:
kill -USR1 "$(pgrep -f 'target/debug/pgfs')"
ls testdata/mnt > /dev/null

The dump is written by the next filesystem operation, here the ls:

INFO pgfs: SIGUSR1 received; state dump will appear on next FUSE callback
INFO getattr{ino=1}: pgfs::fs: state|ino_cache=3 next_ino=4 db=connected (replica none) uptime_secs=41
state|fuse_latency=fuse total=12 p50=<=1kµs p95=<=10kµs p99=<=10kµs
state|db_latency=db total=15 p50=<=1kµs p95=<=1kµs p99=<=10kµs

docs.title: Step 4: read a metrics report
docs.text:
Do some work, then wait for the minute to turn over:

for i in $(seq 1 50); do echo $i > testdata/mnt/m$i; done
rm testdata/mnt/m*

Within 60 seconds, five metrics| lines appear. The metrics|ops line counts the 50 creates and 50 unlinks among the other operations.

docs.title: Step 5: break the database
docs.text:
Stop PostgreSQL underneath the running mount, then touch a name the kernel has not cached:

make db-stop
ls testdata/mnt/after-stop

ls: cannot access 'testdata/mnt/after-stop': Input/output error

This time the first terminal shows an ERROR. Read it left to right: the FUSE operation and its arguments (the span), what pgfs was doing and where (src/db.rs:453), and the root cause reported by PostgreSQL:

ERROR lookup{parent=1 name=after-stop}: pgfs::fs: get attributes of entry "after-stop" in "" (at src/db.rs:453): db error: FATAL: terminating connection due to administrator command

docs.title: Step 6: recover
docs.text:
Start PostgreSQL again, then restart the daemon. pgfs holds a single database connection for its whole lifetime and does not reconnect, so it needs the restart:

./scripts/init_db.sh

Press Ctrl+C in the first terminal. The daemon logs received signal 2; unmounting cleanly and exits. Run ./scripts/pgfs.sh run again, and ls testdata/mnt works.

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
We saw that expected misses stay out of the log, pulled live state out of a running daemon, read its periodic metrics, and followed a real failure from the kernel's bare EIO to its root cause. The reference lists every field; the explanation covers the design.

Generated from spec.app.ObservableDaemon by scripts/build_docs.py. Edit the specification, not this page.

docs.title: Tutorial: On-Demand Profiling
docs.text:
Status: Stable

The SIGUSR2 CPU profiler, the Chrome span trace and scripts/bench_profile.sh ship today behind the profiling Cargo feature. Default builds contain none of it.

Operators can profile a running pgfs daemon without restarting it: SIGUSR2 starts and stops a CPU sampler that writes a flamegraph, and a span trace of every FUSE callback and database call is written on shutdown. All of it is compiled in only with the profiling feature.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

In this tutorial we will build pgfs with profiling compiled in, profile one workload, and open the resulting flamegraph and span trace. We will see where a burst of small writes spends its time.

docs.title: Step 1: build and mount a profiling binary
docs.text:
./scripts/pgfs.sh down
cargo build --release --features profiling
./scripts/ensure_db.sh
mkdir -p testdata/mnt
./target/release/pgfs testdata/mnt 2> testdata/profile-demo.log &
sleep 1
grep 'span trace will be written' testdata/profile-demo.log

INFO pgfs: span trace will be written to /tmp/pgfs-trace-1793059200.json on shutdown

docs.title: Step 2: profile a workload
docs.text:
Start the sampler, run the workload, stop the sampler:

PID=$(pgrep -f 'target/release/pgfs testdata/mnt')
kill -USR2 $PID
for i in $(seq 1 500); do echo "line $i" > testdata/mnt/p$i.txt; done
kill -USR2 $PID
sleep 1
grep 'CPU profiling' testdata/profile-demo.log

INFO pgfs::profiling: CPU profiling started (997 Hz)
INFO pgfs::profiling: CPU profiling stopped; wrote /tmp/pgfs-profile-1793059231.svg and /tmp/pgfs-profile-1793059231.stacks

docs.title: Step 3: open the flamegraph
docs.text: Open the .svg file in a web browser. Each box is a function; its width is the share of samples in which it was on the stack. Hover over the widest towers to find which FUSE callbacks (create, write, flush) and which postgres client calls they lead to. Click a box to zoom into it.

docs.title: Step 4: stop and open the span trace
docs.text:
rm testdata/mnt/p*.txt
kill -TERM $PID
ls -l /tmp/pgfs-trace-*.json | tail -1

Load the JSON file at https://ui.perfetto.dev (or chrome://tracing). Each FUSE callback is a bar, with the db:: spans it caused nested underneath.

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
We profiled a live daemon on demand, without restarting it, and got two complementary views: where CPU time goes (the flamegraph) and where wall-clock time goes (the span trace). For a full scripted run, see the how-to.

Generated from spec.perf.OnDemandProfiling by scripts/build_docs.py. Edit the specification, not this page.

docs.title: Tutorial: Performance Optimizations
docs.text:
Status: Partially implemented

Chunked blocks, prepared statements, asynchronous commit, unlogged tables, per-handle write buffering, transaction batching and the attribute-cache TTL are implemented. Inode-keyed storage, the multi-threaded connection pool and the kernel writeback cache are not. The Reference page has the per-requirement status.

pgfs incorporates a structured performance optimization pipeline targeting database access latency, connection concurrency, userspace buffering, and FUSE kernel-transport tuning.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

In this tutorial we will mount pgfs on a scratch database with two tuning options, --unlogged and --attr-ttl, and measure how many requests the kernel sends with and without attribute caching. We need the project-local cluster running (./scripts/ensure_db.sh).

docs.title: Step 1: create a scratch database and mount it
docs.text:
createdb -h "$PWD/testdata" pgfs_tuning
mkdir -p /tmp/pgfs-tuning
./target/debug/pgfs --conn "host=$PWD/testdata dbname=pgfs_tuning" \
    --unlogged --attr-ttl 0 /tmp/pgfs-tuning 2> /tmp/pgfs-tuning.log &
sleep 1

Because the database is new, --unlogged creates both tables without write-ahead logging:

psql -h "$PWD/testdata" -d pgfs_tuning -Atc \
  "SELECT relname, relpersistence FROM pg_class WHERE relname IN ('entries', 'blocks')"

entries|u
blocks|u

docs.title: Step 2: create some files
docs.text:
mkdir -p /tmp/pgfs-tuning/tree/{a,b,c,d,e}
for d in a b c d e; do for i in $(seq 1 20); do echo x > /tmp/pgfs-tuning/tree/$d/f$i; done; done

docs.title: Step 3: count requests with no attribute cache
docs.text:
We use the state dump's fuse total, the number of FUSE requests served so far. Take one reading, walk the tree three times, and take another:

PID=$(pgrep -f 'pgfs --conn.*pgfs_tuning')
dump() { kill -USR1 $PID; ls /tmp/pgfs-tuning > /dev/null; sleep 0.3;
         grep -o 'fuse_latency=fuse total=[0-9]*' /tmp/pgfs-tuning.log | tail -1; }
dump
for k in 1 2 3; do ls -lR /tmp/pgfs-tuning/tree > /dev/null; done
dump

With --attr-ttl 0 the second total is about 4,200 higher: the kernel asked pgfs about every entry, every time.

docs.title: Step 4: repeat with a 30-second cache
docs.text:
kill -TERM $PID; sleep 1
./target/debug/pgfs --conn "host=$PWD/testdata dbname=pgfs_tuning" \
    --attr-ttl 30 /tmp/pgfs-tuning 2> /tmp/pgfs-tuning.log &
sleep 1
PID=$(pgrep -f 'pgfs --conn.*pgfs_tuning')
dump
for k in 1 2 3; do ls -lR /tmp/pgfs-tuning/tree > /dev/null; done
dump

This time the difference is about 160. The first walk asked pgfs; the next two were answered from the kernel's cache.

docs.title: Step 5: clean up
docs.text:
kill -TERM $PID; sleep 1
dropdb -h "$PWD/testdata" pgfs_tuning
rm -f /tmp/pgfs-tuning.log

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
We created unlogged storage for a throwaway mount and cut the requests for a metadata-heavy workload by more than 95% with one flag. The explanation covers what each option costs.

docs.title: Tutorial: Project-Local Development Environment
docs.text:
Status: Stable

Everything on this page ships today: scripts/init_db.sh, scripts/pgfs.sh, the Makefile targets and the integration suite in scripts/test_*.sh.

A contributor goes from a fresh clone to a live pgfs mount with one command. The Postgres cluster, the mount point, the logs and the pid files all live under the project's testdata/ directory, so nothing touches a system-wide Postgres and rm -rf testdata is a full reset.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

In this tutorial we will go from a fresh checkout to a mounted pgfs filesystem, store a file in it, find that file as rows in PostgreSQL, and take everything down again. It takes about five minutes, most of which is the first compile.

All commands run from the root of the repository.

docs.title: Before we start
docs.text:
pgfs asks the kernel to remove its mount automatically if the daemon ever dies. Unprivileged users may only do that when /etc/fuse.conf allows it. Check:

grep '^user_allow_other' /etc/fuse.conf

If that prints nothing, enable it once:

sudo sed -i 's/^#user_allow_other/user_allow_other/' /etc/fuse.conf

docs.title: Step 1: enter the development shell
docs.text:
nix develop

The shell prints a banner with the Rust, PostgreSQL and FUSE versions it provides. Everything that follows uses those tools.

docs.title: Step 2: bring the filesystem up
docs.text:
./scripts/pgfs.sh up

The first run creates a PostgreSQL cluster in testdata/pgdata, compiles pgfs, and mounts it. The last lines look like this:

pgfs:      starting (log: /path/to/pgfs/testdata/pgfs.log)
mounted:   /path/to/pgfs/testdata/mnt
postgres:  PostgreSQL 17.10 on

Ask the script what is running:

./scripts/pgfs.sh status

mount:     active
daemon:    running (pid 1519591)
postgres:  running

docs.title: Step 3: store a file
docs.text:
mkdir testdata/mnt/tutorial
echo "hello from a database" > testdata/mnt/tutorial/hello.txt
cat testdata/mnt/tutorial/hello.txt

hello from a database

docs.title: Step 4: find the file in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
The file we just wrote is a row in the entries table:

psql -h "$PWD/testdata" -d pgfs -c \
  "SELECT parent, name, kind, size FROM entries WHERE parent = 'tutorial'"

  parent  |   name    | kind | size
----------+-----------+------+------
 tutorial | hello.txt | file |   22

Its 22 bytes of content are a row in the blocks table:

psql -h "$PWD/testdata" -d pgfs -c \
  "SELECT name, block_no, convert_from(data, 'UTF8') FROM blocks WHERE parent = 'tutorial'"

   name    | block_no |     convert_from
-----------+----------+-----------------------
 hello.txt |        0 | hello from a database+
           |          |

docs.title: Step 5: take it down
docs.text:
rm -r testdata/mnt/tutorial
./scripts/pgfs.sh down
./scripts/pgfs.sh status

mount:     none
daemon:    not running
postgres:  running

PostgreSQL keeps running so the next up is quick.

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
We built pgfs, mounted it, wrote a file through the ordinary filesystem interface, and saw the same data as rows in two SQL tables. Next, the Regular Files tutorial explores reading, writing and truncating files in more depth.
