docs.title: Tutorial: Reliable Mount & Shutdown
docs.text:
Status: Stable

AutoUnmount, signal-driven clean unmount, the deadlock watchdog, health files and the pgfs.sh escalation path are all implemented.

The filesystem mounts and unmounts cleanly. Crashing or killing the daemon never leaves a ghost mount behind.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

In this tutorial we will start pgfs, find its health files, stop it politely, then kill it without warning and see that the mount still disappears. Along the way we will see the three layers that keep a mount from becoming a ghost.

docs.title: Step 1: start the daemon and find its health files
docs.text:
./scripts/pgfs.sh up
grep 'health pid file' testdata/pgfs.log | tail -1

health pid file: /tmp/pgfs-5049eced64c2821d.pid

The hash in the name is derived from the mount point. Next to the PID file is a readiness file:

ls /tmp/pgfs-*.pid /tmp/pgfs-*.ready
cat /tmp/pgfs-*.pid

The PID it contains matches ./scripts/pgfs.sh status.

docs.title: Step 2: stop it politely
docs.text:
./scripts/pgfs.sh down

pgfs:      stopping (pid 1519591)
unmounted:  /path/to/pgfs/testdata/mnt

The script sent SIGTERM. The daemon unmounted itself, removed its health files and exited:

grep 'received signal' testdata/pgfs.log | tail -1
ls /tmp/pgfs-*.pid 2>/dev/null || echo "no health files"

docs.title: Step 3: kill it without warning
docs.text:
./scripts/pgfs.sh up
kill -9 "$(cat testdata/pgfs.pid)"
sleep 1
grep testdata/mnt /proc/mounts || echo "mount is gone"

mount is gone

SIGKILL cannot be caught, so the daemon got no chance to clean up. The kernel removed the mount anyway, because pgfs asked for AutoUnmount when it mounted.

docs.title: Step 4: confirm the state is clean
docs.text:
./scripts/pgfs.sh status

mount:     none
daemon:    not running
postgres:  running

Because the daemon was killed, its /tmp health files are still there. They are harmless and are overwritten on the next start.

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
We saw a clean, signal-driven shutdown and an uncatchable kill, and both ended with no mount left behind. The explanation describes why each layer exists.

Generated from spec.app.ReliableMount by scripts/build_docs.py. Edit the specification, not this page.

docs.title: Tutorial: Replicated Storage
docs.text:
Status: Partially implemented

Write routing, lag detection, transparent fallback and the Docker standby work today. File contents (read) are still always served by the primary, and a standby that is unreachable when the daemon starts is dropped for the daemon's lifetime without a warning.

A pgfs mount can be backed by a primary Postgres and a physical streaming standby in Docker. Writes go to the primary; reads are served from whichever node is authoritative at that instant, falling back to the primary when the standby lags. The filesystem is eventually consistent with the standby's lag continuously bounded by the freshness check, and a standby failure never causes data loss or a kernel-visible error.

In this tutorial we will give pgfs a read replica: a second PostgreSQL that follows the first by streaming its write-ahead log. We will mount pgfs with both, see metadata reads go to the replica, then take the replica away and see pgfs carry on without it.

We need Docker, and the project-local cluster from Your first pgfs mount.

docs.title: Step 1: start the standby
docs.text:
./scripts/pgfs.sh down
./scripts/replica_db.sh up

The script copies the primary with pg_basebackup, starts a postgres:17 container on port 5433, and waits until it is streaming:

==> standby is in recovery (streaming)

ready. replica connection string (for --replica):
  host=127.0.0.1 port=5433 dbname=pgfs user=alice

If it reports that the container name /pgfs-replica is already in use, run docker rm pgfs-replica and repeat.

docs.title: Step 2: mount with the replica
docs.text:
mkdir -p testdata/mnt
./target/debug/pgfs --replica "$(./scripts/replica_db.sh conn)" testdata/mnt \
    2> testdata/replica-demo.log &
sleep 1
grep 'replica mode' testdata/replica-demo.log

INFO pgfs: replica mode: reads served from standby (host=127.0.0.1 port=5433 dbname=pgfs user=alice) when fresh

docs.title: Step 3: write, wait, read
docs.text:
mkdir testdata/mnt/replicated
echo "on the primary" > testdata/mnt/replicated/a.txt
sleep 1
ls -l testdata/mnt/replicated

Writes went to the primary. After a moment the standby has replayed them, and the ls (a directory listing plus attribute lookups) is answered by the standby. Ask the daemon:

kill -USR1 "$(pgrep -f 'pgfs --replica')"; ls testdata/mnt > /dev/null
grep 'state|ino_cache' testdata/replica-demo.log | tail -1

... db=connected (replica fresh) ...

docs.title: Step 4: take the standby away
docs.text:
./scripts/replica_db.sh down
ls -l testdata/mnt/replicated
cat testdata/mnt/replicated/a.txt

Both commands still work. The log records the switch once:

WARN pgfs::db: reads falling back to primary (standby stale or unreachable)

docs.title: Step 5: clean up
docs.text:
kill -TERM "$(pgrep -f 'pgfs --replica')"
rm -f testdata/replica-demo.log

The standby's data stays in the Docker volume pgfs-replica-data; ./scripts/replica_db.sh wipe deletes it.

docs.title: What we did
docs.text:
We built a primary/standby pair, mounted pgfs across both, and saw reads move to the standby when it was current and back to the primary when it disappeared, with no error reaching the programs using the mount. The explanation covers the consistency rules behind this.

docs.title: Tutorial: Sharded Filesystem
docs.text:
Status: Planned, not implemented

Specified and designed (design/sharded_filesystem.md), not implemented. The daemon does not accept --shards or --replication-factor, and scripts/shard_db.sh does not exist yet. The tutorial and how-to describe the intended interface.

A pgfs mount can be backed by N independent Postgres host nodes with RAID-5-like subset replication: each directory subtree is pinned to a replication set of R of the N hosts (never a full mirror on every host). Writes fan out to every member of the set; reads consult a quorum and return the newest version. Any number of clients can mount the same namespace from different machines and add files to one shared tree, and a host failure degrades reads and writes to the remaining healthy members without stale or corrupt data.

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation

Preview

This tutorial describes the intended experience once Phase 2 of the roadmap lands. None of its commands work yet.

In this tutorial we will spread one pgfs namespace across five simulated hosts, write files into different subtrees, stop a host and keep working, and mount the same namespace a second time as another client.

docs.title: Step 1: start five hosts
docs.text:
./scripts/shard_db.sh up
./scripts/shard_db.sh conns

Each simulated host is its own PostgreSQL cluster (testdata/pgdata-1 … testdata/pgdata-5). conns prints the comma-separated --shards list.

docs.title: Step 2: mount the namespace
docs.text:
./target/debug/pgfs --shards "$(./scripts/shard_db.sh conns)" \
    --replication-factor 3 testdata/mnt &

The startup log announces the topology:

INFO pgfs: shard topology: 5 hosts, R=3, sets=…

docs.title: Step 3: write into two subtrees
docs.text:
mkdir testdata/mnt/docs testdata/mnt/src
echo hi  > testdata/mnt/docs/a.txt
echo bye > testdata/mnt/src/b.txt

docs and src are top-level names, so each subtree is placed on its own replication set of three hosts. The SIGUSR1 state dump shows which.

docs.title: Step 4: lose a host
docs.text:
pg_ctl -D testdata/pgdata-2 stop
cat testdata/mnt/docs/a.txt testdata/mnt/src/b.txt
echo again >> testdata/mnt/docs/a.txt

Every command still succeeds. Reads and writes need only two of each set's three members. The metrics now report one degraded host.

docs.title: Step 5: bring it back, and add a second client
docs.text:
./scripts/shard_db.sh up        # restarts host 2; it re-syncs
mkdir -p /tmp/client2
./target/debug/pgfs --shards "$(./scripts/shard_db.sh conns)" /tmp/client2 &
cat /tmp/client2/docs/a.txt

The second mount sees the same tree, including the line written while host 2 was down.

docs.title: What we will have done
docs.text:
We will have run one namespace on five hosts with each file on three of them, survived a host failure without errors, and shared the tree between two clients. The explanation describes the design.
